subject: rla
title: Text Structure, Author's Purpose, and Point of View
objectives: You will identify chronological, cause-and-effect, compare-and-contrast, and problem-and-solution structures from signal words and the job of each paragraph.
You will explain how a sentence or paragraph fits into the structure of a whole text, including passages that open out of time order.
You will determine an author's purpose for a whole text and for one part of it, such as an opening scene or a quoted opposing view.
You will describe an author's point of view using word choice, included details, the treatment of opposing views, and the conclusion.
You will identify a narrator's point of view and explain how it shapes what readers know and feel.

slides.title: Text Structure, Author's Purpose, and Point of View
slides.board:
Week 3 · Reasoning Through Language Arts

Today you will:

  • Name four text structures from the job each paragraph does
  • Explain how one part fits the whole, even when a text opens out of order
  • State an author's purpose for a whole text and for one part
  • Describe an author's point of view with evidence
  • Tell how a narrator's point of view shapes what you know

Plan: Warm-up · Structure · Purpose · Point of view · Your turn · GED questions · Recap

notes.say: Weeks 1 and 2 were about what a text says, stated or implied. This week moves to how and why: how the author put the text together, why the author wrote it or included a certain part, and where the author or narrator stands. The GED asks these questions on almost every reading passage, and Social Studies uses the same skills with primary sources. By the end of the hour you should be able to label a passage like a floor plan and back up every answer with words from the text.
ask: When you read a news article, how can you tell whether the writer is just reporting or trying to convince you? (expected: any reasonable answer; listen for word choice or one-sided facts and build on it later)

slides.title: Warm-up: inference review
slides.board:
“Keisha checked the clock for the third time, tapped her pen against the table, and reread the same line of the job application. When her phone buzzed, she grabbed it before the second ring.”

  1. Is Keisha's mood stated or implied?
  2. Infer her mood in one word.
  3. Name two clues that prove it.
  4. Is “Keisha hates her current job” a reasonable inference? Why or why not?
steps: 1. Implied. The text never names a feeling.
2. Nervous, anxious, or impatient (any of these).
3. Any two: checks the clock three times, taps her pen, rereads the same line, grabs the phone before the second ring.
4. No. That is overreach. Nothing in the text mentions her current job.

notes.say: Quick review of week 2. An inference is text clues plus what you know, and every inference has to be proved with words from the text. Give the student about a minute per question. Question 4 checks the overreach trap from last week. Today we will use the same prove-it habit for purpose and point of view: every answer needs evidence.
notes.answer: 1. Implied. 2. Nervous, anxious, or impatient. 3. Any two of the four actions. 4. No: it goes beyond the clues (overreach). She may be waiting for a call about this job, but nothing tells us how she feels about any other job.
notes.watch: If the student answers question 2 with a reason (“she is waiting for a call”) instead of a feeling, ask, “What is she feeling while she waits?”

slides.title: Warm-up: best evidence
slides.board:
Claim: The new evening bus route is popular with riders.

Which detail best supports the claim?

A. The route runs from 6 p.m. to midnight.
B. The city spent $400,000 on two new buses.
C. Ridership on the route doubled in its first three months.
D. Some drivers prefer the evening shift.
steps: A: true but irrelevant. Hours do not show popularity.
B: shows cost, not what riders think.
D: about drivers, not riders.
C is correct. More riders is direct proof the route is popular.

notes.say: Last week's best-evidence checklist: relevant, specific, direct. If the detail is true, does the claim have to be true? Have the student test each choice out loud before you reveal. This prepares today's work, because purpose and point-of-view answers must also be proved with the text.
ask: What question did you ask yourself about each choice? (expected: if this is true, does it prove the claim?)
notes.answer: C. Doubling ridership directly proves popularity. A, B, and D are about the schedule, the cost, and the drivers.

slides.title: Text structure: the floor plan
slides.board:
StructureQuestion it answersSignal words
ChronologicalWhat happened, in what order? What are the steps?first, next, then, later, finally, in 1920
Cause and effectWhy did it happen? What did it lead to?because, since, so, as a result, therefore, led to
Compare and contrastHow are two things alike and different?both, similarly, however, unlike, in contrast, while
Problem and solutionWhat went wrong, and how was it fixed?problem, challenge, solution, answer, proposed

notes.say: Text structure is the pattern an author uses to organize ideas. I like to compare it to the floor plan of a house: once you know the plan, you can predict where things will be. The GED asks about structure in two ways: how a whole passage is organized, and how one sentence or paragraph fits into the whole. Walk through the table one row at a time and ask the student to add one signal word of their own to each row.
ask: Give me one more signal word for cause and effect. (expected: due to, consequently, for this reason, resulted in)
What question does compare and contrast answer? (expected: how two things are alike and different)
notes.watch: Students often think “problem and solution” and “cause and effect” are the same. Point out the difference: a problem-and-solution text has someone doing something to fix a problem.

slides.title: One sentence vs. the whole paragraph
slides.board:
“In 1990, the town of Pine Hollow had three pharmacies. By 2015, two had closed after a large chain store opened on the highway. Because the remaining pharmacy was across town, older residents without cars began skipping refills. In 2019, the county started a free van that runs from the senior center to the pharmacy twice a week.”

What relationship does the third sentence show? What structure organizes the whole paragraph?
steps: Step 1, scope: the first question asks about sentence 3 only.
Step 2, signal word: “Because.” Cause: the only pharmacy was across town. Effect: residents skipped refills. Sentence 3 shows cause and effect.
Step 3, the whole paragraph: label the jobs: background (1990), what went wrong (2015, skipped refills), the fix (2019 van).
Whole paragraph: problem and solution, told in time order. One “because” does not make the whole paragraph cause and effect.

notes.say: Model this one out loud. The trick is scope: the question about one sentence and the question about the whole paragraph have different answers. Read the scope words in the question before you look at the text.
ask: If a question asked about the whole paragraph, why would “cause and effect” be a weaker answer? (expected: it describes one sentence; the paragraph ends with a solution)

slides.title: Signal words are clues, not proof
slides.board:
Ask what job each paragraph does.

  1. Note the scope: sentence, paragraph, or whole passage?
  2. Circle the signal words.
  3. Label each paragraph's job in 2 to 4 words.
  4. Pick the structure that fits all the labels.

Out of order on purpose: many articles open with a dramatic moment, then go back in time (“Before that day…”).

notes.say: Signal words help, but they can mislead. A history article may use “because” once and still be organized by time. So we label the job of each paragraph: “the problem,” “first try,” “result,” “critics.” The labels become a map. Also warn the student that many passages open with a dramatic scene and then jump back. That is not a mistake by the writer; it is a hook. After the hook, the passage usually runs in time order.
ask: A passage opens with a 1910 crash and then describes roads in 1890. Is it out of order by mistake? (expected: no; it opens with a dramatic moment to hook the reader, then goes back to explain)
notes.watch: Watch for students who pick a structure from the first signal word they see. Ask them to label at least two paragraphs before they answer.

slides.title: Label the jobs, then name the structure
slides.board:
[1] For years, the Westfield Community Center had no way to reach families who did not use the internet. [2] Flyers on the center's door reached only people who already visited. [3] Last fall, the center began mailing a one-page newsletter to every home in the neighborhood. [4] Attendance at its free tax-help nights rose from 30 people to 85.

Label each sentence's job. What is the structure?
steps: Sentence 1: the problem (no way to reach some families).
Sentence 2: why the old way failed (flyers reached only regular visitors).
Sentence 3: the fix (a mailed newsletter).
Sentence 4: the result (attendance rose from 30 to 85).
Structure: problem and solution. The last sentence shows the effect of the solution.

notes.say: Here the student watches me label each sentence before I decide. Keep the labels short. When the labels are on the board, the structure almost names itself.
ask: Which sentence would you point to as proof that the solution worked? (expected: sentence 4, attendance rose)

slides.title: What kind of text is this?
slides.board:
(a) First, unplug the coffee maker. Next, fill the tank with water and vinegar. After the cycle, run two tanks of plain water.

(b) Because the Fourth Street bridge closed, traffic on Main Street doubled. As a result, buses ran up to fifteen minutes late.

(c) Both apartments are near the bus line. However, the first allows pets, while the second includes parking.

(d) Many parents who work night shifts cannot find child care. One answer is a center that stays open until midnight.
steps: (a) Chronological / steps: First, Next, After.
(b) Cause and effect: Because, As a result.
(c) Compare and contrast: Both, However, while.
(d) Problem and solution: “cannot find” names a problem; “One answer is” names a solution.

notes.say: Do these together. The student names the structure and the words that gave it away; you reveal one at a time. Point out that (b) also moves forward in time. Many texts mix structures, and the question is which one organizes the ideas.
ask: Which word in (d) tells you a solution is coming? (expected: answer, as in “One answer is”)
notes.answer: (a) chronological; (b) cause and effect; (c) compare and contrast; (d) problem and solution.

slides.title: Maple Court: structure inside structure
slides.board:
Tenants at Maple Court were shocked when the water bill nearly doubled in one year. The manager, Ana Ruiz, suspected leaks but did not know where to look. She started by asking tenants to report dripping faucets and running toilets. Within a month, tenants had reported leaks in 14 of the 40 units. Next, Ruiz hired a plumber to fix them and installed low-flow showerheads. As a result, the next year's bill fell by almost a third.

  1. What structure organizes the whole passage?
  2. Name two time-order words.
  3. What caused the bill to fall?
steps: 1. Problem and solution. Problem: the doubled water bill. Solution: find and fix the leaks.
2. Any two: “started by,” “Within a month,” “Next,” “the next year.”
3. Fixing the leaks and installing low-flow showerheads (signal: “As a result”).

notes.say: Read it aloud, then have the student mark the signal words before answering. This passage shows a common GED pattern: a problem-and-solution text whose solution is told step by step in time order, with a cause and effect at the end.
notes.answer: 1. Problem and solution, with the steps of the solution in time order. 2. Any two of started by, Within a month, Next, the next year. 3. Repairing the leaks in 14 units and installing low-flow showerheads.
notes.watch: If the student says “chronological” for question 1, agree that the steps are in order, then ask, “Why are these steps happening? What are they for?” That leads to the problem and the solution.

slides.title: Author's purpose: make it specific
slides.board:
Three big purposes: inform / explain · persuade · entertain (tell a story)

The author wrote this to verb readers about what exactly.

Weak: “to inform”
Strong: “to explain how one building manager cut a huge water bill”

Persuade? Look for the author urging readers to believe or do something.

notes.say: Everyone learns inform, persuade, and entertain in school, but on the GED that is almost never enough. The choices are specific, and two or three of them may say “explain.” So we use a frame: to do what, about what. Then we check the verb. If the author never asks readers to believe or do anything, “persuade” is wrong, even if the topic is serious.
ask: What is the specific purpose of the Maple Court passage? (expected: to explain how a manager found and fixed leaks to cut the water bill)
Would “to persuade landlords to buy low-flow showerheads” work? (expected: no; the passage never urges anyone to act)
notes.watch: Students choose “persuade” whenever a text has an opinion in it. Ask, “Does the author tell you to believe or do something?”

slides.title: Why is this part here?
slides.board:
The partCommon purpose
Opening story, question, or surprising factTo hook the reader
Statistic, example, quotationTo give evidence for a claim
“Before…” / “Unlike…”To show a change or contrast
“Some people say…”To present an opposing view, often so the author can answer it
Final paragraph or quoteTo show a result or stress the lesson

Look right before and right after the part.

notes.say: The GED loves to ask why an author included one paragraph, one quotation, or one opening scene. The part's purpose depends on its neighbors. A statistic right after a claim is evidence. A “some people say” sentence right before a “but” is an opposing view the author is about to answer. So the habit is: read the sentence before and the sentence after.
ask: An article on a new library begins: “At 9 a.m. on opening day, the line stretched around the block.” Why start there? (expected: to hook the reader and show right away how much people wanted the library)

slides.title: Purpose of a part: the opposing view
slides.board:
“Some people say public pools cost too much to run. It is true that pools are expensive to staff and heat. But a single summer of free swim lessons can prevent drownings, and no budget line is worth more than a child's life.”

Why does the author include the first two sentences?
steps: Step 1, whose idea? Sentence 1 belongs to “some people,” the opponents.
Step 2, the concession: sentence 2 admits part of their point is true (pools are expensive).
Step 3, the turn: “But” signals the author's answer: lessons save lives.
Purpose: to present an opposing view so the author can respond to it. The author's own view: pools are worth the cost.

notes.say: This is the move students most often misread. The author writes the other side's argument in the first two sentences, so a quick reader thinks the author agrees with it. Walk through whose idea each sentence is.
ask: Does the author think pools are cheap? (expected: no; the author admits they are expensive but says they are worth it)
notes.watch: If the student says the author “agrees that pools cost too much,” ask them to find the word where the author turns. Whatever comes after “But” is the author's real position.

slides.title: Purpose: whole and part
slides.board:
Ruiz says the most important step was the first one. “The tenants knew where the problems were,” she said. “I just had to ask.”

(added to the end of the Maple Court passage)

  1. What is the purpose of the whole Maple Court passage? Use the frame.
  2. Why does the author end with Ruiz's quotation?
  3. Is the author's purpose to persuade? Prove it.
steps: 1. To explain how a building manager found and fixed costly leaks.
2. To stress the lesson of the story: the people affected by a problem can help find it.
3. No. The author never urges readers to do or believe anything; the passage reports what happened.

notes.say: Do this one together, with the student doing the talking. Push for specific answers. For question 2, remind them of the table: final paragraphs and quotations often stress the lesson.
notes.answer: 1. To explain how one building manager found and fixed costly leaks (accept: to show how asking tenants helped solve the problem). 2. To stress the lesson, in Ruiz's own words, that the tenants held the key information. 3. No; it informs. There is no call to action.

slides.title: Author's point of view: four clues
slides.board:
Point of view = the author's position or attitude toward the subject.

  1. Word choice: “a reckless plan” vs. “a bold plan”
  2. What is included or left out: only one side's facts?
  3. How others are treated: answered, mocked, or ignored?
  4. The conclusion: where does the author end up?

The author is not everyone quoted. Ask: “Whose words are these?”

notes.say: Authors rarely write “I think.” Their point of view shows in the words they choose, the facts they pick, how they treat people who disagree, and where they land. When you describe a point of view, keep its limits. An author can favor one side and still be fair to the other. And remember that quoting critics is not the same as agreeing with them.
ask: “Reckless” or “bold”: which shows approval? (expected: bold)
An author quotes a critic. How can you tell whether the author agrees? (expected: see whether the author answers the critic, especially after but or however, and what the author concludes)

slides.title: Point of view with limits
slides.board:
“Electric and gas lawn mowers both cut grass well on a typical yard. Gas mowers, however, run longer and handle thick, tall grass more easily. Electric mowers, on the other hand, are quieter, need no oil changes, and start with the push of a button. For a small yard, the electric model is often the better choice.”

Structure? Purpose? Point of view?
steps: Structure: both, however, on the other hand → compare and contrast.
Purpose: sentences 1 to 3 compare; the last sentence recommends. So: to compare the two types and help readers choose.
Point of view: fair to both (gas gets real advantages) but favors electric for small yards.
Distorted: “The author thinks gas mowers are bad.” The text praises gas mowers for big jobs.

notes.say: Model all three questions on one short text. The key teaching point is the last step: the author's point of view has a limit, “for a small yard.” An answer that drops the limit distorts the text.
ask: Which words show the author is fair to gas mowers? (expected: run longer, handle thick, tall grass more easily)

slides.title: Word choice reveals point of view
slides.board:
“The so-called ‘improvement’ plan will tear up a beloved park to build yet another parking garage.”

What is the author's point of view? Which words show it?
steps: “so-called” and the quotation marks around “improvement”: the author doubts it is an improvement.
“tear up” and “beloved”: emotional words that make the loss sound violent and painful.
“yet another”: suggests the town already has too many garages.
Point of view: the author strongly opposes the plan.

notes.say: One sentence can carry a strong point of view. Go word by word and ask what each one adds. Then rewrite the sentence neutrally so the student hears the difference: “The plan would replace part of the park with a parking garage.” Same facts, no attitude.
ask: Rewrite the sentence so it has no point of view. (expected: something like “The plan would replace part of the park with a parking garage.”)

slides.title: Narrator's point of view
slides.board:
Point of viewClueWhat readers learn
First person“I,” “we”: the narrator is a characterOnly the narrator's thoughts. The narrator can be wrong.
Third person limited“he,” “she”; one character's thoughtsOne character's inner life; others seen from outside
Third person omniscient“he,” “she,” “they”; many characters' thoughtsWhat everyone thinks and feels

notes.say: In stories, point of view means who is telling the story and how much that teller knows. First person sounds personal and honest, but a first-person narrator can misjudge people, and readers sometimes understand more than the narrator does. To tell limited from omniscient, count the minds: if the narrator shows the thoughts of only one character, it is limited; if it moves into several characters' heads, it is omniscient.
ask: What can a first-person narrator not tell us directly? (expected: what other characters are thinking)
notes.watch: Students sometimes call any story with dialogue “first person” because characters say “I” in quotation marks. Only the narrator's own “I,” outside quotation marks, makes it first person.

slides.title: How point of view creates a surprise
slides.board: “My brother says he is ‘too busy’ to help me move this weekend. Busy doing what, I wonder. When I called Saturday, he sounded out of breath, and I heard a hammer in the background. He hung up fast. By Sunday night I had carried every box myself. On Monday, a new bookshelf appeared on my porch, its paint still drying, with a note in his handwriting: ‘For the new place.’”
steps: Step 1: “I,” “my,” “me” outside quotation marks → first person.
Step 2, what the narrator believes: the brother is avoiding the move.
Step 3, what the details show: out of breath, a hammer, hanging up fast. He was building something.
Effect: we see only the narrator's thoughts, so we share the narrator's doubt (or guess ahead) until the bookshelf reveals the truth.

notes.say: Model how to answer “How does the point of view affect the reader?” The answer always has two parts: what the narrator believes, and what the details show. The gap between them is where the effect lives.
ask: Retold by an omniscient narrator, what would we know from the start? (expected: that the brother is building a gift, so the surprise would be lost)

slides.title: Which point of view?
slides.board:
(a) “Lena watched her grandfather fold the flag and wondered what he was thinking. He was thinking about the letter in the drawer. He had no idea she had already read it.”

(b) “I told myself the interview went fine. Then I noticed I had my shirt on inside out.”

(c) “Omar counted the bills twice. Something was off, he was sure of it, but the manager only smiled at him.”
steps: (a) Third person omniscient. We get Lena's wondering and her grandfather's thoughts: two minds.
(b) First person. The narrator says “I” and knows only the narrator's own mind.
(c) Third person limited. “He”; we know Omar's thoughts, but the manager is seen only from outside (“only smiled”).

notes.say: Do these together. For each one, the student finds the pronoun clue first, then counts the minds the narrator enters. Reveal after each answer.
notes.answer: (a) third person omniscient; (b) first person; (c) third person limited.
notes.watch: For (a), students often say limited because the passage starts with Lena. Ask, “Whose thoughts does sentence 2 tell us?”

slides.title: Your turn: structure
slides.board:
1. “Unlike city buses, which stop every few blocks, express buses stop only at major stations. Both cost the same, but express buses can cut a long commute by twenty minutes.” Structure? Two signal words.

2. “Heavy rain soaked the fields for three weeks in May. Farmers could not plant on time, so the corn harvest was smaller. Corn prices rose by fall.” Name one cause and one effect.

3. An article begins with a flood in 2021, then says, “Twenty years earlier, the town had voted down a new levee.” Why open this way?
steps: 1. Compare and contrast: any two of Unlike, Both, but.
2. Cause: weeks of rain (could not plant). Effect: smaller harvest, higher prices.
3. To hook the reader with a dramatic event, then go back to explain how it happened.

notes.say: Three minutes. The student works alone while you watch the clock. Then ask for each answer with the evidence.
notes.answer: 1. Compare and contrast (Unlike, Both, but). 2. Any correct pair, such as rain → late planting, late planting → smaller harvest, or smaller harvest → higher prices. 3. To grab attention with the flood and then explain its causes; the passage is not out of order by mistake.
notes.watch: On problem 3, a student may say the passage is “confusing” or “out of order.” Ask what the opening makes a reader want to know.

slides.title: Your turn: purpose and author's point of view
slides.board:
“Critics call the downtown farmers market a nuisance that blocks traffic every Saturday. In fact, the market draws 3,000 shoppers a week, and nearby shops report their best sales on market days. A few hours of detours are a small price for a weekly boost to Main Street.”

1. Why does the author include the first sentence?

2. What is the author's point of view toward the market?

3. Name two word choices that show it.
steps: 1. To present the critics' view so the author can answer it (“In fact”).
2. The author supports the market.
3. Any two: “small price,” “boost,” “In fact” (correcting critics), “best sales.”

notes.say: Three minutes, working alone. Then ask for evidence on every answer: for the purpose question, which word marks the turn; for point of view, which exact words show the attitude. If the student names a feeling without quoting words, ask, “Where does it say that?”
notes.answer: 1. To present an opposing view that the author then answers. 2. The author supports the market and thinks its benefits outweigh the traffic trouble. 3. Any two of “a small price,” “a weekly boost,” “In fact,” “best sales.”
notes.watch: If the student says the author thinks the market is a nuisance, point to “Critics call.” Whose words are those?

slides.title: Your turn: narrator's point of view
slides.board:
“I knew Coach Bell had given up on me. All week he made me run the drills twice while everyone else got water. He never said ‘good job,’ not once. On Friday he handed out the game roster. My name was at the top, next to one word: Captain.”

1. What point of view is this?

2. What does the narrator believe? What do the details show?

3. How does the point of view affect the reader?
steps: 1. First person (“I,” “me,” “my”).
2. The narrator believes Coach Bell has given up on the narrator. The details show the coach was pushing the narrator because he expected more.
3. We see only the narrator's thoughts, so we share the narrator's worry until the roster reveals the truth.

notes.say: Three minutes, then check. This is the same pattern as the bookshelf story, so the student should be able to use the two-part answer: what the narrator believes, and what the details show.
notes.answer: 1. First person. 2. The narrator believes the coach has given up; the extra drills and the captain role show the coach was preparing the narrator to lead. 3. Limited to the narrator's mind, readers share the narrator's doubt, and the ending surprises them.

slides.title: GED question: relationship between paragraphs
slides.board:
[2] For decades, Riverside's only grocery store sat on the far side of the highway. Residents without cars paid for taxis or bought food at gas stations.

[3] In 2020, a group of neighbors opened a co-op market in an empty bank building. Within a year, it had 900 member households.

How does paragraph 3 relate to paragraph 2?

A. It gives a second example of the problem in paragraph 2.
B. It describes a response to the problem in paragraph 2.
C. It compares two grocery stores in Riverside.
D. It explains what caused the problem in paragraph 2.
steps: A is wrong: paragraph 3 is not another hardship; it shows neighbors doing something.
C is wrong: the passage never compares the two stores' prices, size, or goods.
D is wrong: the cause (store far away, no car) is already in paragraph 2. Paragraph 3 comes after the problem.
B is correct: paragraph 2 = the problem; paragraph 3 = the co-op that answers it.

notes.say: Treat this like the real test. Have the student label each paragraph's job before reading the choices, then eliminate together, saying the reason for each cut.
ask: Label paragraph 2 and paragraph 3 in two words each. (expected: “the problem,” “the solution”)
notes.answer: B. Paragraph 2 describes the problem (no nearby grocery), and paragraph 3 describes the neighbors' solution (the co-op).

slides.title: GED question: author's point of view
slides.board:
“Supporters of the four-day school week say it saves money. It does save a little: the district expects to spend about 2 percent less. But that small saving comes at a large cost to working parents, who must now find child care every Friday.”

Which statement best describes the author's point of view?

A. The author believes the four-day week saves the district a great deal of money.
B. The author thinks the four-day week's savings do not justify its burden on parents.
C. The author argues that schools should stay open on weekends.
D. The author has no opinion and simply reports both sides.
steps: A is wrong: it confuses the supporters' claim with the author's; the author calls the saving “small” and “a little.”
C is wrong: weekends are never mentioned. It is not stated.
D is wrong: “But,” “small saving,” and “large cost” show a clear opinion.
B is correct: the author admits a small saving, then argues the cost to parents outweighs it.

notes.say: Remind the student: find the author's own words, especially after the turn. Then cut the choices that confuse the supporters with the author, go beyond the text, or ignore the word choice.
ask: Which word marks the turn to the author's own view? (expected: But)
notes.answer: B. The author concedes a 2 percent saving but calls it small next to the large cost to working parents.

slides.title: GED question: effect of the narrator's point of view
slides.board:
Recall the coach story (“I knew Coach Bell had given up on me…”).

How does the first-person point of view affect the story?

A. It lets readers know the coach's plans from the beginning.
B. It makes readers share the narrator's mistaken belief until the roster reveals the truth.
C. It shows that the narrator cannot be trusted about any event in the story.
D. It lets the narrator explain what every player on the team is thinking.
steps: A is wrong: a first-person narrator cannot see the coach's thoughts. We learn his plan only at the end.
C is wrong: it goes too far. The narrator misjudges the coach's feelings, but the events (extra drills, the roster) are reported plainly.
D is wrong: that describes an omniscient narrator, not an “I” narrator.
B is correct: we are inside the narrator's head, so we share the narrator's doubt until the ending.

notes.say: Point-of-view effect questions always come back to what the narrator can and cannot know. Eliminate with that in mind.
notes.answer: B. Limited to the narrator's thoughts, readers share the narrator's belief that the coach has given up until the roster shows otherwise.

slides.title: GED strategy: map the passage
slides.board:
1. Read the question first. Note the scope: sentence, paragraph, or passage.
  2. Spend 30 seconds labeling each paragraph in 2 to 4 words: “hook: 1883,” “problem,” “fix,” “critics,” “law.”
  3. Answer structure and purpose questions from your map.
  4. For “why include” questions, read before and after the part.
  5. For point of view, ask: “Whose words are these?”

notes.say: On test day, the clock matters. Rereading a 500-word passage for every question wastes minutes. A paragraph map, written on the erasable board you get at the test, lets you answer most structure and purpose questions by glancing at your labels. Practice it this week on every passage, even short ones, until it takes less than a minute.
ask: Why read the question before labeling the paragraphs? (expected: to know the scope and what to look for)

slides.title: Recap and next steps

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
In weeks 1 and 2 you worked on what a text says: its main idea and what it implies. This week you will look at how and why a text says it. On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, many questions ask how a passage is organized, why the author included a certain part, or what the author or narrator thinks. In this lesson you will learn to:

  • name the four common text structures from the job each paragraph does
  • explain how one sentence or paragraph fits into the whole, even when a passage opens out of time order
  • state an author's purpose for a whole text and for one part of it
  • describe an author's point of view with evidence from the text
  • identify a narrator's point of view and explain how it shapes what you know

Work one screen at a time. Most screens end with a check question. If you miss one, you will see exactly why that answer is wrong. Then you will move on to Practice and the Exit Check.

screens.title: Text structure: the floor plan of a text
screens.html:
Text structure is the pattern an author uses to organize ideas. Think of it as a floor plan: once you know it, you can predict where things will be. Most GED passages use one or more of these four structures.

StructureWhat it doesSignal words
Chronological (time order, sequence)Tells events or steps in the order they happenfirst, next, then, later, finally, before, after, in 1920
Cause and effectExplains why something happened or what it led tobecause, since, so, as a result, therefore, led to, due to
Compare and contrastShows how two or more things are alike and differentboth, similarly, likewise, however, unlike, in contrast, while
Problem and solutionDescribes a problem and one or more ways to fix itproblem, challenge, solution, answer, proposed, solved

check.prompt: Drag each signal word or phrase to the structure it usually signals.
check.hint: For each phrase, ask: does it tell when, why, how things are alike or different, or how something gets fixed?
check.explain: Chronological: “after that” tells when. Cause and effect: “as a result” introduces an effect; “due to” introduces a cause. Compare and contrast: “in contrast” shows a difference; “similarly” shows a likeness. Problem and solution: “one solution is” introduces a fix.
check.why: The most common mistake is putting “after that” under Cause and effect. “After” tells when something happened, not why, so it signals time order.

screens.title: Chronological order, and passages that open out of order
screens.html:
A chronological text tells events or steps in time order. Dates and time words (in 1920, later, by the next spring) are the clues.

Watch for one twist: many articles open with a dramatic moment and then go back in time to explain how it happened. Phrases like Before that day or Twenty years earlier mark the jump back. The opening is a hook, not a mistake. After it, the passage usually runs in time order.

When a question asks what happened first, use the dates and time words, not the order of the paragraphs.

example.prompt:
“The night the Mill River dam failed, water swept through the valley in minutes. Years before, the mill owners had lowered the dam to build a road across its top. An engineer had warned them that the spillway was too small. The warning was ignored.”

Which event happened first: the dam failing or the owners lowering the dam?
steps: The passage opens with the dam failing. That is the hook.
“Years before” jumps back in time to the owners lowering the dam.
The engineer's warning also came before the failure, while the dam still stood.
example.answer: The owners lowering the dam happened years before the failure, even though the failure is told first.

check.prompt:
“On opening day in 2019, more than 600 people lined up outside the new Eastside Library. The idea had started in 2012, when a group of parents began collecting signatures. Three years later, voters approved the money to build it.”

Why does the author begin with opening day instead of with the parents in 2012?
check.hint: Check the dates. Which event actually happened first? Then ask what a crowd of 600 people does for a reader.
check.explain: Opening day (2019) is told first, but it happened last. “The idea had started in 2012” jumps back in time. Authors open with a vivid moment, such as 600 people in line, to hook readers, then explain the history. The most tempting wrong answer says opening day came first, but the dates prove it came seven years after the signatures.
options: to catch the reader's interest with a striking scene before explaining how the library came to be
to show that the library was built quickly, in the same year that the parents began their effort
because opening day was the first event in the story, before the parents began collecting signatures
to argue that the parents' signatures mattered less to the project than the vote three years later
why: You missed the dates. The parents began in 2012 and the library opened in 2019, seven years later, so it was not built in the same year the effort began.
You took the order of the sentences as the order of events. “Had started in 2012” shows the jump back in time: opening day came last.
You read an opinion into the passage. The author never compares the importance of the signatures and the vote; the opening is a hook, not an argument.

screens.title: Cause and effect
screens.html:
A cause is why something happens. An effect is what happens as a result. Some signal words introduce the cause (because, since, due to); others introduce the effect (so, as a result, therefore, led to).

Effects can form a chain: one effect becomes the cause of the next. “Heavy rain delayed planting, so the harvest was small, and corn prices rose.” Rain causes late planting; late planting causes a small harvest; a small harvest causes higher prices.

To check a cause-and-effect pair, put it in this frame: “____ happened because ____.” If the sentence makes sense and matches the text, you have it right.

check.prompt:
“The factory on Route 9 closed in March. As a result, the diner across the street lost most of its lunch customers.”

Type the two- or three-word signal phrase that introduces the effect.
check.hint: Find the words that connect the two sentences.
check.explain: The cause is the factory closing. The phrase “As a result” introduces the effect: the diner lost its lunch customers. Check it with the frame: “The diner lost customers because the factory closed.” It makes sense.

mistakes.why: “Because” introduces a cause, and it does not appear in these sentences. Look for the phrase right before what happened to the diner.
“Closed” is part of the cause (the factory closing), not a signal phrase. The signal phrase links the two events: look at the start of the second sentence.
“Lost” is part of the effect itself. The question asks for the signal phrase that introduces the effect.

screens.title: Compare and contrast: block and point by point
screens.html:
A compare-and-contrast text shows how two or more things are alike and different. Writers organize it in one of two ways:

  • Block: everything about subject A in one paragraph, then everything about subject B in the next. Watch for a paragraph that opens “B works differently.”
  • Point by point: one feature at a time for both subjects (cost of A and B, then time for A and B).

Signal words: both, similarly, likewise, also (alike); however, unlike, in contrast, while, on the other hand (different).

check.prompt:
“A certificate program teaches students mainly in classrooms and usually lasts one year or less. Students pay tuition and must find an employer after they finish.

An apprenticeship works differently. Apprentices are hired by an employer from the start and learn mostly on the job. They earn a paycheck while they train, but the training often takes three to five years.”

How are these two paragraphs organized?
check.hint: Does each paragraph talk about one path or both?
check.explain: Paragraph 1 is entirely about certificate programs; paragraph 2 opens “An apprenticeship works differently” and is entirely about apprenticeships. One subject per paragraph is a block comparison. Point by point is tempting because the paragraphs cover the same features (where students learn, cost, length), but each paragraph sticks to one subject.
options: block comparison: each paragraph fully describes one training path
point by point: the cost of both paths, then the length of both paths
chronological order: the steps of a career, from classroom to first job
problem and solution: a shortage of workers, then a plan to train more
why: Point by point would discuss both paths inside each paragraph, one feature at a time. Here each paragraph covers only one path.
You noticed time words like “after they finish,” but the paragraphs describe two different paths, not one sequence of steps.
No shortage of workers is described, and nobody proposes a plan. The paragraphs set two options side by side.

screens.title: Problem and solution
screens.html:
A problem-and-solution text describes something that went wrong and how someone fixed it or could fix it. It often has three parts: the problem, the solution (sometimes after a failed first try), and the result.

Do not mix it up with cause and effect. Both talk about why things happen, but in a problem-and-solution text, someone takes action to fix the problem. Words like problem, challenge, difficulty, solution, answer, proposed, fixed, and one way to are the clues.

check.hint: Which sentence describes something the clinic did?
check.explain: Sentences 1 and 2 describe the problem: long waits that drove patients away. Sentence 3 describes the action the clinic took, reserved times. That is the solution. Sentence 4 shows the result.
spans: Patients at the Grove Street clinic often waited more than two hours to see a doctor.
Many gave up and left before being seen.
Last spring, the clinic began letting patients reserve a time online or by phone.
Average waits have since dropped to twenty minutes.
check.why: The most common wrong click is the last sentence. It shows the result of the solution (shorter waits), not the action the clinic took.

screens.title: Signal words are clues, not proof
screens.html:
A single signal word does not decide the structure. A history article can use “because” once and still be organized by time. To find the structure, ask what job each paragraph does.

  1. Read the question and note its scope: one sentence, one paragraph, or the whole passage.
  2. Circle the signal words in that part.
  3. Label each paragraph's job in two to four words (“the problem,” “first try,” “result”).
  4. Choose the structure that fits all the labels in the question's scope.

Many passages mix structures: a problem-and-solution article may tell its solution step by step in time order. The structure of the whole is the pattern that ties every paragraph together.

example.prompt:
“In 1990, Pine Hollow had three pharmacies. By 2015, two had closed after a chain store opened on the highway. Because the remaining pharmacy was across town, older residents without cars began skipping refills. In 2019, the county started a free van to the pharmacy twice a week.”

What structure organizes the whole paragraph?
steps: Labels: background (1990); what went wrong (closings, skipped refills); the fix (2019 van).
“Because” in sentence 3 shows one cause-and-effect link, but it is only one sentence.
The pattern that ties all four sentences together is a problem and a response to it.
example.answer: Problem and solution, told in time order.

check.prompt:
“Sea levels along the Carver coast have risen about eight inches since 1950. During storms, high water now floods Harbor Road several times a year, cutting off the only route to the hospital. In 2021, the town raised a two-mile stretch of the road by three feet. Last winter, for the first time in a decade, the road stayed open through every storm.”

Which structure best describes how the whole paragraph is organized?
check.hint: Label what each sentence does. Does someone take action?
check.explain: Label the jobs: the problem (rising seas flood the road to the hospital), the solution (the town raised the road), and the result (the road stayed open). Problem and solution fits every sentence. Cause and effect is the most tempting choice, but it describes only the first two sentences.
options: problem and solution, with a result
cause and effect, because rising seas flood the road
compare and contrast of 1950 and today
chronological steps for raising a road
why: Rising seas causing floods is one link in the paragraph, but the town also acts (raising the road) and the paragraph ends with the result. Label all four sentences before you choose.
1950 is mentioned only to measure the rise. The paragraph never sets two things side by side to show likenesses and differences.
The paragraph never explains how to raise a road. It moves through time, but the job of each sentence is problem, fix, and result.

screens.title: How one part fits the whole
screens.html:
Many GED questions ask how a sentence or paragraph relates to another part, or how it fits into the passage. Common relationships:

The part…Clue
introduces the problem that later paragraphs solveproblem, could not, failed
gives an example or evidence for the claim before itfor example, numbers, quotations
explains a cause of what came beforebecause, since, due to
shows a result or effectas a result, so, since then
presents a contrast or an opposing viewhowever, but, some people say
moves the story forward or back in timelater, by 1918, before that day

Label the two parts first; the relationship is usually the link between your labels.

check.prompt:
[1] “Every summer, the Lakeview pool closed for weeks because it could not hire enough lifeguards. [2] In 2022, the city began paying for lifeguard training for any teenager who agreed to work two summers. [3] The pool has not closed a single day since.”

Complete the statement.

Sentence 2 {{0}}, and sentence 3 {{1}}.
check.hint: Give each sentence a two-word label first: problem, solution, or result?
check.explain: Label the jobs: sentence 1 = the problem (pool closes, no lifeguards); sentence 2 = the solution (paid training); sentence 3 = the result (no closings since). So sentence 2 describes a solution to the problem in sentence 1, and sentence 3 shows the result of that solution.

options: describes a solution to the problem in sentence 1
gives another example of the problem in sentence 1
explains what caused the lifeguard shortage
compares Lakeview with other city pools
why: Sentence 2 is not another hardship. It describes something the city did about the shortage.
Sentence 2 never says why lifeguards were scarce; it describes the city's response.
No other pool is mentioned, so nothing is being compared.

options: shows the result of that solution
states the problem the passage will solve
presents an opposing view of the training plan
returns to the time before the plan began
why: The problem was stated in sentence 1. Sentence 3 comes after the fix and tells what happened next.
No one disagrees with the plan in this paragraph. Sentence 3 reports what happened after it.
“Since” points forward from the plan to now, not back to the time before it.

screens.title: Author's purpose: make it specific
screens.html:
An author writes to inform or explain, to persuade, or to entertain (tell a story). GED answer choices are more specific than that, so finish this frame:

The author wrote this to verb readers about what exactly.

Then test the verb. A text is persuasive only if the author tries to make readers believe or do something: watch for should, must, we need to, or strong judgments. A text that reports what happened, even a serious or exciting event, is informative.

Finally, choose the answer that fits the whole text. A purpose that fits only one paragraph is too narrow.

check.prompt:
A passage describes how a city hired a team to plant 2,000 trees, explains how the trees were chosen, and reports that summer sidewalk temperatures dropped on the planted streets. It never tells readers what to do.

Which statement best describes the author's purpose?
check.hint: Does the author ever tell readers what they should do? Which choice covers the whole passage?
check.explain: The passage explains a program from start to finish (hiring, choosing trees, results) and never urges readers to act. The purpose that covers the whole text is to explain how a city planted trees and what changed after it did. The persuade choice is tempting because the results sound good, but reporting a success is not the same as urging others to copy it.
options: to explain how a city planted trees and what changed after it did
to persuade other cities to plant thousands of trees on their streets
to entertain readers with the story of one tree planter's summer
to inform readers about the best kinds of trees for hot city streets
why: You saw a good result and assumed the author is urging others to copy it. The passage never says other cities should act, so its purpose is to explain.
The passage covers a whole program, not one person's experience, and it is reporting facts rather than telling a story.
This is too narrow. Choosing the trees is one part of the passage; it also covers the planting and the cooler sidewalks.

screens.title: Why did the author include this part?
screens.html:
The GED often asks why an author included one part of a text: an opening story, a statistic, a quotation, or a whole paragraph. Common answers:

  • to hook the reader: a story, question, or surprising fact at the start
  • to give evidence or an example for a claim
  • to show a contrast or a change
  • to present an opposing view, often so the author can answer it
  • to show a result or stress the lesson, often at the end

A part's purpose depends on its neighbors. Read the sentence right before it and right after it.

example.prompt:
“Some people say public pools cost too much to run. It is true that pools are expensive to staff and heat. But a single summer of free swim lessons can prevent drownings, and no budget line is worth more than a child's life.”

Why does the author include the first two sentences?
steps: Sentence 1 is the opponents' idea (“Some people say”), not the author's.
Sentence 2 admits part of it is true. Then “But” turns to the author's answer.
So the first two sentences set up a view the author is about to answer.
example.answer: To present an opposing view so the author can respond to it. The author's own view is that pools are worth the cost.

check.prompt:
“Maria Lopez used to spend two hours a day on three buses to reach her job at the hospital. Since the county added an express route last year, her trip takes forty minutes. The new route now carries 1,800 riders a day, and the county plans to add two more.”

Why does the author include the details about Maria Lopez?
check.hint: Look at what comes after Maria's story. How does her example connect to it?
check.explain: Maria's two-hour trip shrinking to forty minutes puts a human face on the route's effect. Then the author widens the view with 1,800 daily riders. Opening with one person's experience is a common way to hook readers and give an example. Nothing in the paragraph argues for free passes or contrasts Maria with other riders.
options: to show, through one rider's experience, what the express route changes
to argue that hospital workers deserve a free pass on county buses
to explain why the county decided to add exactly two more express routes
to contrast Maria's trip with the trips of the route's other riders
why: You added an argument the text does not make. Free passes are never mentioned; Maria's story illustrates the route's effect.
The paragraph never explains why the county chose two more routes. Maria's details describe her trip, not the county's plans.
The paragraph never describes other riders' trips, so nothing is being contrasted. It gives the total riders, which supports Maria's story rather than opposing it.

screens.title: Author's point of view: the clues
screens.html:
An author's point of view is the author's position or attitude toward a subject. Authors rarely write “I think,” so look for four clues:

  • Word choice: “a reckless plan” and “a bold plan” describe the same plan very differently.
  • What is included or left out: does the author give only one side's facts?
  • How others are treated: are opposing views answered fairly, mocked, or ignored?
  • The conclusion: where does the author end up?

To test word choice, try swapping a word for a neutral one. If the meaning stays the same but the feeling disappears, the original word was showing the author's attitude.

check.skill: Author's point of view: word choice
check.prompt:
“The city council's latest scheme would hand a beloved neighborhood park to a developer for a luxury hotel. The park covers four acres and includes a playground and two ball fields. Residents have until May 1 to comment.”

Which two words or phrases most clearly reveal the author's attitude toward the plan? Select two answers.
check.hint: Swap each choice for a plain word. Which swaps change the feeling of the sentence?
check.explain: “Scheme” suggests a sneaky or dishonest plan; a neutral writer would say “plan” or “proposal.” “Beloved” makes the park sound precious, so losing it sounds like a loss. Together they show the author opposes the plan. The size, the ball fields, and the date are facts any writer could include.
options: scheme
beloved
four acres
two ball fields
until May 1
why: “Four acres” is a neutral fact about the park's size. It would read the same in an article for or against the plan.
“Two ball fields” is a neutral fact. It describes the park without showing how the author feels.
“Until May 1” is a neutral date. It tells readers a deadline but carries no attitude.

screens.title: Does the author agree with everyone quoted?
screens.html:
Authors often quote or describe people who disagree with them. That does not mean the author agrees. To decide where the author stands:

  1. Ask, “Whose words are these?” Look for critics say, some argue, opponents claim.
  2. Look for a turn: but, however, yet, in fact, still. What comes after the turn is usually the author's own view.
  3. Notice a concession: an author may admit that part of the other side is true (“It is true that…”) before answering it. Admitting a point is not the same as agreeing overall.
  4. Check the conclusion.

check.skill: Author's point of view: opposing views
check.prompt:
“Critics of the new bike lanes on Elm Street say they have made traffic worse. Rush-hour drives along Elm do take about two minutes longer than before. However, crashes on the street have dropped by half, and bike trips have tripled. Two minutes is a fair trade for a street where no one gets hurt.”

Which statement best describes the author's point of view?
check.hint: Find the turn word. What does the author say after it?
check.explain: Sentence 1 gives the critics' view. Sentence 2 is a concession: drives really are two minutes longer. “However” turns to the author's answer (fewer crashes, more bike trips), and the conclusion calls the delay “a fair trade.” The author supports the lanes while admitting the small cost. The most tempting wrong answer copies the critics' view from the first sentence.
options: The author supports the bike lanes, even though they add a little time to drives.
The author agrees with critics that the bike lanes have made Elm Street worse.
The author has no opinion and is simply listing facts about the bike lanes.
The author thinks that cars should be kept off Elm Street during rush hour.
why: You took the critics' words as the author's. “However” marks the turn, and the author ends by calling two minutes “a fair trade.”
“A fair trade” is a judgment, and the facts are arranged to answer the critics, so the author does have a point of view.
This goes beyond the text. The author never suggests banning cars; the point is that two extra minutes is worth fewer crashes.

screens.title: Describing a point of view accurately
screens.html:
Once you know where an author stands, describe it exactly, no stronger and no weaker than the text. Watch for three traps in the answer choices:

  • Too strong: the author prefers electric mowers for small yards, but the choice says the author thinks gas mowers are bad.
  • Confused with others: the choice gives the view of a critic the author quotes.
  • Not stated: the choice adds a plan or opinion the author never mentions.

Keep the author's limits: words like for a small yard, often, in most cases, and for now matter.

check.prompt:
“Paper and digital bus passes both get riders on board quickly. Paper passes, however, need no phone and never run out of battery. Digital passes, on the other hand, can be reloaded from home and replaced for free if a phone is lost. For riders who take the bus every day, the digital pass is usually the better choice.”

Which statement best describes the author's point of view?
check.hint: Find the author's recommendation. What words limit it?
check.explain: The author gives each pass real advantages (paper: no phone needed, no battery to die; digital: reload from home, free replacement), then recommends digital for riders who take the bus every day. The accurate answer keeps both the fairness and the limit. The choice saying paper passes are a poor choice for nearly every rider is the most tempting, but it drops the limit and ignores the praise for paper passes.
options: The author sees strengths in both passes but favors the digital pass for daily riders.
The author believes paper passes are a poor choice for nearly every kind of rider.
The author thinks digital passes will soon replace paper passes on most bus lines.
The author has no preference and leaves the choice of pass entirely to readers.
why: This is too strong. The author says paper passes need no phone and never run out of battery, and the recommendation is limited to daily riders.
This is not stated. The author makes no prediction about the future of either pass.
The last sentence gives a clear recommendation: for daily riders, the digital pass is “usually the better choice.”

screens.title: Narrator's point of view
screens.html:
In a story, point of view means who tells the story and how much that teller knows.

Point of viewClueWhat readers learn
First personThe narrator says “I” or “we” and is a characterOnly the narrator's own thoughts. The narrator can be mistaken.
Third person limited“He,” “she”; the thoughts of one characterOne character's inner life; everyone else seen from outside
Third person omniscient“He,” “she,” “they”; the thoughts of several charactersWhat many characters think and feel

Only the narrator's own “I” counts. Characters say “I” inside quotation marks in every kind of story. To tell limited from omniscient, count the minds the narrator enters.

check.prompt:
“Lena watched her grandfather fold the flag and wondered what he was thinking. He was thinking about the letter in the drawer. He had no idea that she had already read it.”

Is this first person, third person limited, or third person omniscient? Type your answer.
check.hint: First check the pronouns. Then count how many characters' thoughts you learn.
check.explain: The narrator uses “she” and “he,” so it is third person. Then count the minds: we learn what Lena wonders and what her grandfather is thinking, and even what he does not know. Two minds means third person omniscient.

mistakes.why: The narrator tells us what Lena wonders and what her grandfather is thinking. Entering two characters' minds makes it omniscient, not limited.
The narrator never says “I.” Lena and her grandfather are “she” and “he,” so the story is in the third person.

screens.title: How the narrator's point of view shapes the story
screens.html:
GED questions often ask how the point of view affects what readers understand. Answer in two parts:

  1. What the narrator believes or knows.
  2. What the details actually show.

A first-person narrator sees only from inside one head, so readers share that person's guesses, worries, and mistakes. When the details point one way and the narrator believes another, the story can build suspense or end with a surprise. An omniscient narrator, by contrast, can let readers know more than any one character does.

Be careful not to go too far: a narrator who misjudges a person is not lying about every event.

example.prompt:
“I could tell the new manager did not like me. She kept asking how I organized the stockroom and wrote down everything I said. On Friday, she called a staff meeting. ‘Starting Monday,’ she announced, ‘every store in the district will use Mario's stockroom system.’”

How does the point of view affect the reader?
steps: “I” outside the quotation marks: first person. The narrator is Mario.
Mario believes the manager dislikes him. The details (questions, notes, adopting his system) show she admired his work.
Because we see only Mario's thoughts, we share his worry until the announcement.
example.answer: The first-person point of view keeps readers inside Mario's mistaken belief, so the ending is a surprise.

check.skill: Effect of narrator's point of view
check.prompt:
“My neighbor never waved back. For a year I waved every morning, and every morning he stared past me. I decided he was the rudest man on Birch Street. Then one day I saw him at the clinic, a white cane folded in his lap, and the nurse called out, ‘Mr. Hale? The eye doctor will see you now.’”

How does the first-person point of view affect the story?
check.hint: What does the narrator believe for most of the story? When do readers learn something different?
check.explain: The narrator says “I” and knows only one mind. The narrator believes Mr. Hale is rude. The white cane and the eye doctor suggest he could not see the waving. Because readers see only the narrator's view, they share that judgment until the clinic scene. The choice saying readers cannot believe any event is tempting, but misjudging one person does not make every reported event false.
options: Readers share the narrator's mistaken view of Mr. Hale until the clinic scene suggests the real reason he never waved.
Readers know from the beginning that Mr. Hale cannot see, because the narrator explains his thoughts in the opening lines.
Readers cannot believe any event the narrator reports, since the narrator has already been wrong about the neighbor once.
Readers learn how every person on Birch Street feels about Mr. Hale, because the narrator describes all of their thoughts.
why: A first-person narrator cannot see into Mr. Hale's mind, and nothing in the opening explains his thoughts. The truth comes out only at the clinic.
This goes too far. The narrator misjudged Mr. Hale's reasons, but the events the narrator reports (the waving, the cane, the nurse) are told plainly.
This describes an omniscient narrator. The narrator shares only one mind, the narrator's own, and never mentions what other neighbors think.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
Here are the rules to carry into Practice:

  • Text structure is how an author organizes ideas: chronological, cause and effect, compare and contrast (block or point by point), or problem and solution.
  • Signal words are clues, not proof. Note the scope of the question, label the job of each paragraph, and choose the structure that fits them all.
  • A passage that opens with a dramatic moment and then jumps back in time is using a hook. Use dates, not paragraph order, to put events in order.
  • Author's purpose: “to ___ readers about ___.” Persuade only if the author urges readers to believe or do something. For a part, read before and after it.
  • Author's point of view: word choice, what is included, how others are treated, the conclusion. Ask, “Whose words are these?” and keep the author's limits.
  • Narrator's point of view: first person, third limited, third omniscient. Count the minds. A first-person narrator can be wrong, and that gap creates suspense or surprise.

Next: Practice Set A (15 questions). Score 80% or higher on first tries to master it; otherwise take Set B. Then take the Exit Check.

stimuli.title: Setting the Nation's Clocks
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] On November 18, 1883, people in many American towns lived through what is sometimes called “the day of two noons.” In city after city, when the clocks reached twelve, railroad workers and jewelers stopped them, waited several minutes, and started them again, or turned the hands back so that noon arrived a second time. Nothing about the sun had changed. What had changed was the way the country agreed to tell time.

[2] Before that day, most towns kept their own local time. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest in the sky over that particular town. Because the sun appears to move from east to west, noon arrived a little later with every mile a traveler went west. When it was noon in one town, it might be a few minutes past noon in a town to the east and a few minutes before noon in a town to the west. For people who rarely traveled more than a few miles from home, these small differences hardly mattered.

[3] The railroads changed that. As train lines stretched across the country in the decades after the Civil War, local time became a serious problem. Each railroad set its schedules by the time in its home city or at its major stations, so a single station might display several clocks, each showing a different railroad's time. By the early 1880s, railroads in the United States were using dozens of different time standards. Travelers missed connections because they misread schedules. Worse, when two trains shared a single track, a difference of even a few minutes between the crews' watches could lead to a deadly collision.

[4] Several people proposed solutions. Around 1870, a New York school principal named Charles Dowd suggested dividing the country into bands, or zones, each one hour apart, with every clock inside a zone showing the same time. In the end, the railroads acted on their own rather than waiting for the government. A railroad official named William F. Allen drew up a plan that placed the nation's rail lines into four main time zones. The railroads agreed to switch to the new system at noon on November 18, 1883. That decision produced the day of two noons.

[5] Not everyone welcomed the change. Some town leaders and newspaper writers complained that private companies had no right to decide what time it was. Critics described sun time as natural and honest, and they mocked the new system as “railroad time.” A number of towns kept their local time for years. Over time, however, as more businesses, schools, and courts followed the railroad schedules, standard time became the time most people actually lived by.

[6] Congress finally made the system official in 1918, when it passed the Standard Time Act. The law gave a federal agency the power to set the boundaries of the time zones, and the same law created daylight saving time for the first time in the nation's history. Today, most people never stop to think that their clocks show the same time as clocks hundreds of miles away. That agreement, which seems so natural now, began as a practical answer to a dangerous problem on the rails.

stimuli.title: The Torque Wrench
stimuli.source: Original fiction written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] Walt Brenner had not said more than ten words to me in my first two weeks at Delgado's Garage, and six of them were “Do it again. Do it again.”

[2] He said it on my first Monday, when I rotated the tires on a delivery van and he walked over, crouched by the front wheel, and ran his thumb across each lug nut as if he were reading Braille. He said it again on Thursday, after I changed the oil in a pickup and left a smear of grease on the fender. I wiped the fender. He did not say thank you.

[3] “He's like that with everybody,” said Marisol, who ran the front counter and had worked there longer than anyone except Walt. I did not believe her. I had watched him joke with the parts delivery driver and lend his good flashlight to Kenny, the other new hire, who once dropped a socket wrench into an engine and spent an hour fishing it out. Nobody told Kenny to do it again.

[4] By the end of the second week, I had decided that Walt simply did not think I belonged under a car, or maybe that a woman did not, and I had started rehearsing what I would say to Mr. Delgado when I quit.

[5] On Friday I did a brake job on a minivan that belonged to a woman with three car seats in the back. I took my time. I checked every bolt with the torque wrench, twice, and wrote the numbers on the work order the way Walt did, in small square print. When I rolled out from under the van, Walt was standing there reading my numbers. He picked up the wrench, checked one wheel himself, and set the wrench down on the bench.

[6] “Okay,” he said, and walked away.

[7] I was so angry I almost missed what happened next. Walt went into the office, and through the open door I saw him take the clipboard with next month's schedule off its nail. He crossed something out and wrote above it. Then he hung the clipboard back up and went to lunch.

[8] When he was gone, I looked. Every Saturday in March had said “Brakes and alignment: W. Brenner.” Now, on the last two Saturdays, his name had a line through it. Above it, in that small square print, was mine.

[9] Kenny's name was not on the schedule at all.

stimuli.title: Draft Newsletter Article: Two Paths into the Trades
stimuli.source: Original document written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
Eastside Career Center Monthly Newsletter
Draft article (for review)

(1) Many adults who want a career in the skilled trades face the same question: should they enroll in a certificate program at a community college, or should they look for an apprenticeship? Both paths can lead to steady, well-paying work as an electrician, plumber, welder, or heating and cooling technician. The two paths differ, however, in how people learn, how they pay, and how long they train.

(2) A certificate program teaches students mainly in classrooms and campus workshops. Many programs last one year or less, so graduates can begin looking for jobs quickly. (A) certificate students do not have a job waiting for them; they must find an employer on their own after they finish. They also usually pay tuition, although many qualify for financial aid.

(3) An apprenticeship works differently. Apprentices are hired by an employer or a union from the start, and they learn mostly on the job under an experienced worker, with some classroom hours added. (B) they earn a paycheck while they train, apprentices usually do not take on student debt. Apprenticeships take longer to complete, however, often three to five years, and openings can be hard to get.

(4) Which path is right depends on the person. (C) someone who needs to finish training within a year may prefer a certificate, while someone who needs to earn money during training may prefer an apprenticeship. Our career counselors can help you weigh your choices. Call the front desk to schedule a free appointment.

stimuli.title: Five Digits That Changed the Mail
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] On July 1, 1963, a smiling cartoon mail carrier began appearing in post offices, newspapers, and television ads across the United States. He was called Mr. ZIP, and his job was to teach Americans a new habit: adding a five-digit number to the end of every address. The number was the ZIP Code, short for Zone Improvement Plan. Within a few years, most Americans would write it without a second thought, but in 1963 it was a strange request.

[2] For most of the nation's history, mail was sorted entirely by hand. Clerks stood in front of walls of wooden slots, read each address, and tossed each letter into the right slot. A skilled clerk memorized thousands of streets and towns. The system worked as long as the amount of mail stayed manageable and experienced clerks stayed on the job.

[3] That changed in the twentieth century. As the country grew, hand sorting could no longer keep up with the mail. Businesses began sending bills, catalogs, and advertisements to customers all over the country, and the amount of mail grew rapidly. During World War II, many experienced clerks left to serve in the military, and their replacements did not know the sorting schemes by heart. The new clerks needed more time to sort each letter, and the old system began to strain.

[4] The Post Office tried a partial fix first. In 1943, it divided many large cities into numbered delivery zones, so a letter might be addressed to “Chicago 6, Illinois.” The zones helped clerks inside those cities, but they did nothing to speed mail moving between cities and towns. In 1963, postal officials introduced a nationwide plan. Under the ZIP Code system, the first digit stood for a broad region of the country, the next two digits narrowed the location to a central mail-processing area, and the last two digits pointed to a local post office or delivery zone. A letter's route could now be read from a single number instead of a full address.

[5] At first, many people ignored the new codes. Some writers complained that the government was turning citizens into numbers, and others simply saw no reason to change. Nevertheless, the Post Office kept up its campaign, and in 1967 it began requiring ZIP Codes on large bulk mailings sent by businesses. As companies added the codes to their mailing lists, ordinary letter writers followed.

[6] The ZIP Code also made it easier for machines to help sort the mail, because a number is far simpler for a machine to read than a handwritten street name. In 1983, the U.S. Postal Service, as the Post Office had been renamed, added four more digits, creating “ZIP+4,” to direct mail to a small area such as one side of a city block or a single large building. Today, the five digits that once puzzled Americans are among the most familiar numbers in daily life. They remain a simple answer to what had become an overwhelming problem.

stimuli.title: Tuesdays and Thursdays
stimuli.source: Original fiction written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] For three months, my son Andre had been lying to me, and I was tired of pretending not to notice.

[2] It started in September. Every Tuesday and Thursday at six he said, “Going to Kev's,” grabbed his backpack, and was out the door before I could ask what a twenty-four-year-old needed a backpack for at a friend's house. He came home after nine, ate standing at the counter, and went straight to his room.

[3] Then there were the phone calls. Twice I heard him say, “I don't think I'm ready,” and once, “Don't tell my dad.” When I walked into the kitchen, he hung up.

[4] “He's grown, Ray,” my sister Denise told me when I called her. “Let him have his business.” But Denise had not raised him alone after his mother passed. She had not spent seven years watching him drift between warehouse jobs since he left high school in the eleventh grade.

[5] In November I ran into Kevin at the gas station and asked how their Tuesdays were going. He looked at me as if I had asked about the weather on the moon. That night I decided I would ask Andre straight out, and I practiced what I would say: calm at first, and then not so calm.

[6] I never got to say it. When I came downstairs Saturday morning, there was a sheet of paper on the kitchen table, held flat by the salt shaker. It was a printed report listing four subjects, and next to each one, a score and the word “Passed.” Stuck to the report was a note in his careful block letters: “Tuesdays and Thursdays, Adult Learning Center. Your turn, Pop. They have a spot for you in January.”

[7] I read it three times. Then I went to find my reading glasses, because I wanted to read it again.

stimuli.title: Draft Newsletter Article: Day Shift or Night Shift?
stimuli.source: Original document written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
Harmon Distribution Center Employee Newsletter
Draft article (for review)

(1) Every spring, Harmon Distribution Center opens new full-time positions on both the day shift and the night shift, and every spring employees ask the same question: which shift is the better choice? Both shifts offer the same benefits and the same base pay. They differ, though, in extra pay, in the work itself, and in how they fit with life outside the warehouse.

(2) The day shift runs from 7:00 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. Most of the center's trucks arrive during these hours, so the work is fast-paced, with a steady stream of pallets to unload. (A) the shift ends in the middle of the afternoon, day-shift workers usually have their evenings free for family, classes, or a second job. Day positions are popular, so they fill quickly, and employees with the most seniority are chosen first.

(3) The night shift runs from 10:00 p.m. to 6:30 a.m. (B) the day shift, it is quieter, with fewer trucks and more time spent restocking shelves and preparing orders for the morning. Night-shift workers also earn an extra $2.00 per hour on top of base pay. The schedule can be hard on sleep and family life, however, and some workers find it difficult to adjust.

(4) Which shift is better depends on what matters most to you. An employee who is saving for a car might choose nights for the extra pay, while a parent who wants to be home for dinner might choose days. (C) the choice comes down to whether extra pay or a daytime schedule matters more to you. Human Resources can show you which positions are open on each shift. Applications are due April 15.

items.prompt: What is the author's main purpose in this passage?
items.hint: Use the frame “The author wrote this to ___ readers about ___.” Does the author ever ask readers to do or believe something?
items.explain:
Step 1. Look at what each paragraph does: it describes the switch in 1883, explains local time, explains the problems the railroads faced, describes the solution, reports the critics, and tells how the system became law in 1918.

Step 2. All of this explains a piece of history: how standard time began and why. The author never urges readers to act. The correct choice is the one about explaining how and why the country came to use standard time zones.

Step 3. Check the distractors. The passage does not argue for a return to sun time; the critics' views are reported, not adopted. No specific crash is described; paragraph 3 says only that a time difference “could lead to” a collision. The passage gives no instructions for setting a clock.
options: to explain how and why the United States came to use standard time zones
to persuade readers that the country should go back to keeping local sun time
to entertain readers with the story of a deadly railroad crash in the year 1883
to instruct readers on how to set their clocks to the correct time zone
why: You took the critics' view in paragraph 5 as the author's. The author only reports it, and the conclusion calls standard time “a practical answer.”

You remembered the word “collision” from paragraph 3. It says a time difference “could lead to” a crash; no actual crash in 1883 is described, and the passage is history, not a story told to entertain.
