The passage tells the history of time zones but never gives steps for setting a clock. Explaining how something began is not the same as giving instructions.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes how paragraphs 3 and 4 are organized?
items.hint: What goes wrong in paragraph 3? What do people do about it in paragraph 4?
items.explain:
Step 1. Label paragraph 3. It says local time “became a serious problem” and lists what went wrong: many clocks at one station, missed connections, and possible collisions. Its job: the problem.

Step 2. Label paragraph 4. It opens with “Several people proposed solutions” and describes Dowd's idea and Allen's plan, which the railroads adopted. Its job: the solution.

Step 3. Together, the paragraphs follow a problem and solution structure. The critics choice is tempting because it is a real part of the passage, but it describes paragraph 5.
options: Paragraph 3 describes a problem with local time, and paragraph 4 explains the solution people proposed and adopted.
Paragraph 3 compares sun time with railroad time, and paragraph 4 explains why most travelers came to prefer sun time.
Paragraphs 3 and 4 list, step by step, how a station worker set each of the station's several clocks every day.
Paragraphs 3 and 4 present the complaints of the town leaders and newspaper writers who opposed the new time zones.
why: Neither paragraph says anyone preferred sun time. Paragraph 3 explains what went wrong with local time, and paragraph 4 describes the fix.
You noticed “several clocks” in paragraph 3, but the passage never explains how anyone set them. That detail is part of the problem, not a set of steps.
These are the critics from paragraph 5, not paragraphs 3 and 4. Check the scope of the question before you answer.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from paragraph 3 that states the problem that the rest of the paragraph explains.
items.hint: One sentence uses the word “problem.” Do the other sentences give details about it?
items.explain:
Step 1. Look for the sentence that names the problem in general terms: “As train lines stretched across the country…, local time became a serious problem.”

Step 2. Check that the other sentences explain it. Several clocks at one station, dozens of time standards, missed connections, and possible collisions are all details showing why local time was a problem.

Step 3. Check the traps. “The railroads changed that” is a transition. The collision sentence is the most dramatic, but it is only one example.
spans: The railroads changed that.
As train lines stretched across the country in the decades after the Civil War, local time became a serious problem.
Each railroad set its schedules by the time in its home city or at its major stations, so a single station might display several clocks, each showing a different railroad's time.
By the early 1880s, railroads in the United States were using dozens of different time standards.
Travelers missed connections because they misread schedules.
Worse, when two trains shared a single track, a difference of even a few minutes between the crews' watches could lead to a deadly collision.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the collision sentence. It is the most dramatic detail, but it is only one example of the problem. Another common miss is “The railroads changed that,” a transition that links back to paragraph 2 without naming the problem.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 3, what was one effect of each railroad setting its schedules by the time in its own home city or major stations?
items.hint: Find the signal word “so” in paragraph 3. What comes right after it?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the cause in paragraph 3: “Each railroad set its schedules by the time in its home city or at its major stations.”

Step 2. The signal word so introduces the effect: “a single station might display several clocks, each showing a different railroad's time.” The correct choice is the one about several clocks at one station.

Step 3. Check the distractors. Congress did not act until 1918. Towns did not stop keeping local time because of this; paragraph 5 says many kept it for years. The passage never mentions separate tracks.
options: A single station might display several clocks, each showing a different time.
Congress quickly passed a law requiring every town to use standard time.
Towns across the country soon stopped keeping their own local sun time.
Railroads began building separate tracks so that trains would never share a line.
why: You connected the problem to the law in paragraph 6, but Congress did not act until 1918, decades later, and the passage never says it acted quickly.
You assumed the railroads' choice ended local time. Paragraph 5 says many towns kept local time for years, even after 1883.
You built on the collision detail, but the passage never mentions separate tracks. It says only that shared tracks made time differences dangerous.

items.prompt: The passage does not tell events in the order they happened. Put these events in the order in which they actually occurred. Drag each event to its position.
items.hint: Paragraph 1 is a hook. Find a date or time clue for each event: “Before that day,” “Around 1870,” 1883, and 1918.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find a time clue for each event.

  • Towns keep sun time and few people notice: paragraph 2 describes local time, and paragraph 3 says “The railroads changed that” in the decades after the Civil War. 1st.
  • Dowd's suggestion: “Around 1870” (paragraph 4). 2nd.
  • The railroads switch: November 18, 1883 (paragraphs 1 and 4). 3rd.
  • The Standard Time Act: 1918 (paragraph 6). 4th.

Step 2. Notice the trap. The passage opens with the day of two noons, so a reader who follows the order of the passage might place 1883 first. The author starts there to hook the reader, then goes back in time.
choices: Congress passes the Standard Time Act.
Charles Dowd suggests dividing the country into time zones one hour apart.
Before the railroads spread across the country, towns set their clocks by the sun, and few people notice the small differences.
The railroads switch to four main time zones, creating the day of two noons.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the day of two noons first because the passage opens with it. Paragraph 1 is a hook; paragraph 2 begins “Before that day” and goes back in time.

items.prompt: Why does the author begin the passage by describing “the day of two noons” instead of beginning with how towns kept local time?
items.hint: Think about how a strange or surprising scene affects a reader. What does paragraph 2 do right after it?
items.explain:
Step 1. Notice the structure. Paragraph 1 describes a strange moment in 1883. Paragraph 2 then begins “Before that day” and goes back in time.

Step 2. Opening with an unusual event (clocks striking noon twice) makes readers curious. The rest of the passage answers the question it raises: why did that happen? The correct choice is the one about catching the reader's interest with a surprising event.

Step 3. Check the distractors. One day cannot show a slow change. The author says the change solved “a dangerous problem,” so the author is not arguing that it created confusion. The passage never claims sun time was more accurate.
options: to catch the reader's interest with a surprising event, then explain the history behind it
to show that the change to standard time happened slowly, a little at a time over many years
to argue that the railroads created needless confusion when they changed the nation's clocks
to prove that local sun time was more accurate than the time the railroads chose to keep
why: The day of two noons was a single day, so it cannot show a slow change. Paragraph 5 describes the slow acceptance, not paragraph 1.
The author calls the change “a practical answer to a dangerous problem.” The confusion came from the old system, not from the switch.
You took the critics' description of sun time as “natural and honest” as the author's view. The passage never claims sun time was more accurate.

items.prompt:
Read the draft newsletter article. Then choose the transition that best completes each blank in these excerpts.

Paragraph 2, blank (A): Many programs last one year or less, so graduates can begin looking for jobs quickly. {{0}} certificate students do not have a job waiting for them; they must find an employer on their own after they finish.

Paragraph 3, blank (B): {{1}} they earn a paycheck while they train, apprentices usually do not take on student debt.

Paragraph 4, blank (C): Which path is right depends on the person. {{2}} someone who needs to finish training within a year may prefer a certificate, while someone who needs to earn money during training may prefer an apprenticeship.
items.hint: Decide how each sentence relates to the one before it: a contrast, a cause, or an example. Then pick the transition that signals that relationship.
items.explain:
Blank (A). The sentence before gives an advantage (graduates can look for jobs quickly). The next gives a drawback (no job is waiting). An advantage followed by a drawback is a contrast, so “However,” is correct. “As a result” is the most tempting, but nothing in a short program causes students to lack a job.

Blank (B). Earning a paycheck is the reason apprentices avoid debt: cause and effect. “Because” introduces the cause.

Blank (C). The first sentence makes a general point (the right path depends on the person). The next gives two specific people as illustrations. “For example,” introduces an illustration.

options: However,
As a result,
Similarly,
For instance,
why: “As a result” says the short program causes students to lack a job. Finishing quickly does not cause that; the sentence turns from an advantage to a drawback.
“Similarly” signals a likeness, but the sentence gives a drawback after an advantage. That is a contrast.
“For instance” introduces an example of the sentence before. Having no job waiting is not an example of finishing quickly.

options: Because
Although
Unless
Until
why: “Although” signals a surprise or contrast. Earning a paycheck and avoiding debt go together; one explains the other.
“Unless” makes it a condition (“if they do not earn a paycheck”), which reverses the meaning.
“Until” sets a time limit that the paragraph never states.

options: For example,
In contrast,
Otherwise,
Meanwhile,
why: “In contrast” signals a difference from the sentence before, but this sentence explains the general point by giving two cases.
“Otherwise” means “if not,” a condition the paragraph does not set up.
“Meanwhile” signals something happening at the same time. The sentence illustrates a point; it does not move through time.

items.prompt: How does the writer organize paragraphs 2 and 3 of the draft article?
items.hint: Paragraph 1 promises to explain how the two paths “differ.” What does each of the next two paragraphs describe?
items.explain:
Step 1. Label each paragraph. Paragraph 2 describes certificate programs: where students learn, how long it takes, finding a job, and tuition. Paragraph 3 describes apprenticeships on the same points.

Step 2. Paragraph 1 says the paths “differ,” and paragraph 3 opens with “An apprenticeship works differently.” These are compare-and-contrast signals. One subject per paragraph is a block comparison.

Step 3. The article never gives steps for becoming an electrician, never describes a worker shortage, and mentions student debt only once.
options: by describing one training path in each paragraph so that readers can compare the two
by listing, in time order, the steps a person must follow to become a licensed electrician
by describing a shortage of skilled workers in paragraph 2 and a way to fix it in paragraph 3
by explaining the causes of student debt in paragraph 2 and its effects on workers in paragraph 3
why: Electricians are named once in paragraph 1 as one possible career. The article never gives steps for becoming one.
You looked for a problem and a fix, but the article never mentions a worker shortage. The paragraphs describe two options side by side.
You built on one detail: student debt is mentioned once, in paragraph 3, as a difference between the paths. It is not the organizing idea of both paragraphs.

items.prompt: Paragraph 5 first reports the critics' complaints and then turns to explain what actually happened. Type the one word in paragraph 5 that signals this turn.
items.hint: Look for a contrast word like the ones on the compare-and-contrast list.
items.explain: Paragraph 5 opens with the critics: they “complained,” called sun time “natural and honest,” and “mocked” railroad time. Then the sentence “Over time, however, as more businesses, schools, and courts followed the railroad schedules…” turns to what actually happened. However is a contrast signal: what follows pushes against what came before. “Over time” is nearby, but it signals time, not contrast.

mistakes.why: “Over time” tells when things changed; it is a time signal. The word that marks the turn away from the critics comes right after it.
“Complained” describes what the critics did. It is part of the opposing view, not a signal word that turns away from it.
“Mocked” describes how the critics treated the new system. Look for the contrast word that introduces what happened instead.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the point of view from which the story is told?
items.hint: Who says “I” in the story? Does the story ever tell us directly what Walt is thinking?
items.explain:
Step 1. The narrator uses “I” and “me” (“ten words to me,” “I rotated the tires”), so the story is in the first person.

Step 2. Identify the narrator: a new worker in her first two weeks. She is not Walt, because she describes Walt from the outside, and not Marisol, because Marisol speaks to her.

Step 3. Ask what the narrator can know. She tells her own feelings (“I was so angry”) but never Walt's thoughts; she can only watch what he does. The omniscient choice is tempting because the story includes several characters, but we enter only one mind.
options: It is told in the first person by a new mechanic who shares her own thoughts but can only guess at Walt's.
It is told in the third person by a narrator who reveals the thoughts of Walt, Marisol, and the new mechanic.
It is told in the first person by Walt, who explains to readers why he is strict with every new employee.
It is told in the third person by Marisol, who watches the other workers from her place at the front counter.
why: The narrator says “I” and “me,” so the story is in the first person. We never learn what Walt or Marisol is thinking.
Walt never explains himself; he barely speaks. The “I” describes Walt from the outside, so she cannot be Walt.
Marisol speaks to the narrator in paragraph 3, so she is a character, not the storyteller. And the narrator says “I.”

items.prompt:
Complete the statement about the passage.

In paragraph 5, the author {{0}}. Paragraph 6 then {{1}}.
items.hint: Give paragraphs 5 and 6 a two- or three-word label each. Whose views are in paragraph 5?
items.explain:
Paragraph 5. Label it: “critics.” It reports complaints from town leaders and newspaper writers, then turns with “however” to show that standard time won out anyway. So it presents an opposing view and then shows that it did not win out. The tempting wrong answer copies the critics' argument, but those are their words, not the author's.

Paragraph 6. Label it: “law: 1918, today.” Congress made the system official, and today people take it for granted. That is the final result. The last sentence echoes paragraph 3, but only to sum up.

options: presents an opposing view and then shows that it did not win out
argues that private companies had no right to decide what time it was
compares sun time and railroad time point by point to show which is better
lists the steps that towns followed to switch over to standard time
why: This is the critics' argument, which the author reports (“Some town leaders and newspaper writers complained”). The author then turns with “however.”
Paragraph 5 does not weigh the two kinds of time feature by feature. It reports how critics described them and then what happened.
Paragraph 5 says some towns kept local time for years; it never gives steps for switching.

options: shows the final result: the system became law and is now taken for granted
returns to the danger of train collisions described earlier in paragraph 3
gives more of the critics' reasons for preferring local sun time
explains in detail how Charles Dowd's original plan worked
why: Paragraph 6 mentions “a dangerous problem on the rails” only in its last sentence, to sum up. Its main job is the 1918 law and the result today.
The critics do not appear in paragraph 6. It moves forward to 1918 and the present.
Dowd's plan is in paragraph 4. Paragraph 6 is about the Standard Time Act and today.

items.prompt: The narrator believes that Walt does not think she belongs at the garage. Which two details suggest that Walt actually trusts her work? Select two answers.
items.hint: Look for what Walt does at the end of the story, after he checks her brake job. Which details compare her to the other new hire in a way that favors her?
items.explain:
Step 1. Focus on actions that show trust, not friendliness. Trust at a garage means being given important work.

Step 2. Walt replaces his own name with the narrator's for brake and alignment work, which is safety work, right after checking her careful brake job. Correct.

Step 3. The final line, “Kenny's name was not on the schedule at all,” contrasts her with the other new hire. Walt was friendlier to Kenny, but he chose the narrator for the work. Correct.

Step 4. The flashlight shows friendliness to Kenny, Marisol's comment explains Walt's manner, and the missing thank-you is part of the narrator's case against Walt.
options: Walt crosses his own name off the March schedule for brakes and alignment and writes hers above it.
Kenny's name does not appear on the schedule at all.
Walt lends his good flashlight to Kenny.
Marisol says that Walt is “like that with everybody.”
Walt does not say thank you after the narrator wipes the grease off the fender.
why: Lending the flashlight shows Walt is friendly to Kenny. It says nothing about whether he trusts the narrator's work, and the narrator uses it as evidence that Walt favors Kenny.
Marisol's comment suggests Walt's strictness is not personal, but it does not show he trusts the narrator's work.
This is part of the narrator's evidence that Walt dislikes her. It does not show trust.

items.skill: Effect of narrator's point of view
items.prompt: How does the first-person point of view affect the reader's experience of the story?
items.hint: What does the narrator believe for most of the story? When do readers learn something that changes that belief?
items.explain:
Step 1. In first person, readers see only the narrator's thoughts. For most of the story, she believes Walt does not think she belongs (paragraph 4) and plans to quit.

Step 2. Walt's thoughts are never shown. Readers learn his real opinion only through an action at the end: he gives her his brake and alignment shifts.

Step 3. So the point of view creates a surprise and shows the gap between what the narrator believes and what is true. The choice saying readers cannot trust any event is tempting, but misjudging one person does not make every reported event false.
options: Readers know only the narrator's thoughts, so they share her belief that Walt dislikes her until his actions reveal otherwise.
The narrator explains Walt's thoughts throughout, so readers know from the start that he plans to give her his Saturday shifts.
The narrator is angry, so readers cannot trust any of the events she describes, including the change to the March schedule.
The story is told by Marisol, so readers learn how everyone at the garage really feels about the two new employees.
why: A first-person narrator cannot see into Walt's mind, and this narrator never does. Readers learn his plan only from the schedule at the end.
This goes too far. An angry narrator may misjudge people, but she reports actions like the schedule change plainly, and nothing suggests they are false.
Marisol is a character who speaks to the narrator; she is not the storyteller. The “I” is the new mechanic.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the author's point of view toward the adoption of standard time?
items.hint: Reread the last sentence of the passage. What words does the author use to describe standard time in the author's own voice?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the author's own words, not the critics'. The conclusion calls standard time “a practical answer to a dangerous problem on the rails,” and paragraph 3 calls local time “a serious problem.” These word choices show the author views standard time favorably.

Step 2. Look at how the critics are treated. Paragraph 5 reports their complaints, then turns with “however.” The author reports the objection but does not adopt it.

Step 3. The choice saying the author agrees with the critics confuses their view with the author's. The Congress choice is not stated, and the “unnecessary” choice distorts paragraph 2.
options: The author sees standard time as a sensible fix for a real problem and reports the critics without agreeing.
The author agrees with the critics that private companies should not have been allowed to decide the time.
The author believes that Congress, not the railroads, should have created the nation's time zones in 1883.
The author thinks standard time was unnecessary because towns' clocks differed by only a few minutes.
why: You took the critics' words as the author's. The author reports them (“Critics described…”) and then turns with “however” to show standard time won out.
This is not stated. The author says the railroads acted “rather than waiting for the government” but never says the government should have acted first.
This distorts paragraph 2. Small differences “hardly mattered” only for people who rarely traveled; paragraph 3 explains they became dangerous on the railroads.

items.skill: Purpose of a part; narrator's point of view
items.prompt:
Complete the statements about the story.

The author ends the story with the sentence “Kenny's name was not on the schedule at all” in order to {{0}}. Because the story is told in the first person, readers learn Walt's real opinion of the narrator only through {{1}}.
items.hint: Remember how Walt treated Kenny earlier. In a first-person story, how can readers learn what another character thinks?
items.explain:
Blank 1. Walt was friendlier to Kenny (the flashlight), so the narrator assumed he preferred Kenny. The last line shows that Walt chose the narrator, not Kenny, for important work. It confirms what the schedule change suggests. Saying Kenny is about to be fired goes beyond the text.

Blank 2. The narrator says “I” and knows only her own mind. Walt barely speaks (“Okay”), so readers learn his opinion only through his actions: checking her work and putting her name on the schedule.

options: confirm that Walt chose the narrator over the friendlier new hire
show that Kenny is about to be fired from Delgado's Garage
suggest that Walt dislikes both new employees equally
introduce a new conflict between Kenny and the narrator
why: This goes beyond the text. Being left off one month's schedule does not mean Kenny is being fired; the story never says so.
This distorts the ending. Walt just gave the narrator his own shifts, so he does not dislike her.
Kenny never reacts in the story, and the story ends here. The line closes the story; it does not open a new conflict.

options: his actions, such as changing the schedule
his thoughts, which the narrator describes
Marisol's explanation of how he feels
a talk he has with Mr. Delgado
why: A first-person narrator cannot see inside Walt's head, and this one never claims to.
Marisol says only that Walt is “like that with everybody.” She never explains his opinion of the narrator.
Mr. Delgado is mentioned only as the person the narrator planned to tell when she quit. Walt never talks to him in the story.

items.prompt: What is the author's main purpose in this passage?
items.hint: Label what each paragraph does. Does the author ever ask readers to do or believe something?
items.explain:
Step 1. Label the paragraphs: 1, hook (Mr. ZIP in 1963); 2, hand sorting; 3, the problem; 4, first fix and the ZIP Code; 5, resistance and acceptance; 6, results today.

Step 2. Together they explain a piece of history: why the ZIP Code was needed and how it caught on. The author never urges readers to do anything. The correct choice is the one about explaining why the ZIP Code was created and how Americans came to use it.

Step 3. The persuade choice copies the critics' complaint. Mr. ZIP is only the hook. The passage gives no steps for looking up a code.
options: to explain why the ZIP Code was created and how Americans came to use it
to persuade readers that the government should stop turning citizens into numbers
to entertain readers with a story about the cartoon character named Mr. ZIP
to instruct readers on how to look up the correct ZIP Code for an address
why: You took the critics' complaint in paragraph 5 as the author's view. The author reports it and then shows the codes won out.
Mr. ZIP appears only in the opening paragraph as a hook. The passage as a whole is history, not a story told to entertain.
The passage explains what the digits stand for, but it never tells readers how to find a code. Explaining a system is not giving instructions.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes how paragraphs 3 and 4 are organized?
items.hint: What goes wrong in paragraph 3? What does the Post Office do about it in paragraph 4?
items.explain:
Step 1. Label paragraph 3: hand sorting “could no longer keep up,” mail grew, experienced clerks left, and the old system began to strain. Its job: the problem.

Step 2. Label paragraph 4: “tried a partial fix first” (city zones in 1943), then a nationwide plan (the ZIP Code in 1963). Its job: the solutions.

Step 3. Together they follow a problem and solution structure. The critics choice describes paragraph 5.
options: Paragraph 3 describes a problem with hand sorting, and paragraph 4 describes the fixes the Post Office tried.
Paragraph 3 compares mail in cities with mail in towns, and paragraph 4 explains why towns got mail faster.
Paragraphs 3 and 4 list, step by step, how a clerk sorted letters into the wooden slots in a post office.
Paragraphs 3 and 4 present the complaints of writers who thought the government was turning people into numbers.
why: Paragraph 4 mentions mail moving between cities and towns, but neither paragraph compares the two or says towns got mail faster.
The wooden slots are in paragraph 2, and even there the passage does not give sorting steps. Check the scope of the question.
These complaints are in paragraph 5, not paragraphs 3 and 4. Check which paragraphs the question names.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from paragraph 3 that states the problem that the rest of the paragraph explains.
items.hint: Which sentence states, in general terms, what went wrong? Do the other sentences give reasons or results?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the sentence that names the problem in general terms: “As the country grew, hand sorting could no longer keep up with the mail.”

Step 2. Check that the others explain it: more mail from businesses and fewer experienced clerks are the reasons hand sorting fell behind, and slower sorting by new clerks is the result.

Step 3. “That changed in the twentieth century” is a transition that links back to paragraph 2.
spans: That changed in the twentieth century.
As the country grew, hand sorting could no longer keep up with the mail.
Businesses began sending bills, catalogs, and advertisements to customers all over the country, and the amount of mail grew rapidly.
During World War II, many experienced clerks left to serve in the military, and their replacements did not know the sorting schemes by heart.
The new clerks needed more time to sort each letter, and the old system began to strain.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the last sentence, because a strained system is easy to picture. That sentence shows the result of the problem. Another common miss is “That changed in the twentieth century,” a transition that does not name the problem.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 3, what was one effect of experienced clerks leaving to serve in the military during World War II?
items.hint: Find the sentence about World War II. What does it say happened because the clerks left?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the cause in paragraph 3: experienced clerks “left to serve in the military.”

Step 2. The same sentence gives the effect: “their replacements did not know the sorting schemes by heart.” That in turn led to the next effect: sorting took longer, and the old system began to strain.

Step 3. The ZIP Code came in 1963, decades later. Businesses sent more mail, not less. Machines appear only in paragraph 6.
options: Their replacements did not know the sorting schemes by heart.
The Post Office soon introduced the five-digit ZIP Code nationwide.
Businesses stopped mailing catalogs and bills to customers far away.
Machines took over the work of sorting the mail in large cities.
why: You jumped ahead to paragraph 4. The ZIP Code came in 1963, about twenty years after the war, and the passage does not call it a direct result of the clerks leaving.
This reverses the text. Paragraph 3 says businesses sent more and more mail, not less.
Machines are mentioned only in paragraph 6, as something the ZIP Code later made easier. Nothing in paragraph 3 says machines took over.

items.prompt: The passage does not tell events in the order they happened. Put these events in the order in which they actually occurred. Drag each event to its position.
items.hint: Paragraph 1 is a hook. Find a date or time clue for each event: “For most of the nation's history,” 1943, 1963, 1967, 1983.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find a time clue for each event.

  • Hand sorting: “For most of the nation's history” (paragraph 2), before any zones or codes. 1st.
  • City delivery zones: 1943 (paragraph 4). 2nd.
  • Mr. ZIP and the ZIP Code: July 1, 1963 (paragraphs 1 and 4). 3rd.
  • ZIP Codes required on large business mailings: 1967 (paragraph 5). 4th.
  • ZIP+4: 1983 (paragraph 6). 5th.

Step 2. The passage opens in 1963 to hook the reader, then goes back. Use dates, not paragraph order.
choices: Mr. ZIP appears as the five-digit ZIP Code is introduced.
Four more digits are added, creating ZIP+4.
Clerks sort every letter by hand, memorizing thousands of streets and towns.
The Post Office begins requiring ZIP Codes on large business mailings.
Many large cities are divided into numbered delivery zones.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting Mr. ZIP first because the passage opens with him. Paragraph 1 is a hook set in 1963; paragraph 2 goes back to how mail was sorted before any codes existed.

items.prompt: Why does the author begin the passage with Mr. ZIP's first appearance in 1963 instead of with how clerks sorted the mail by hand?
items.hint: What does paragraph 2 do right after the opening? How does a cartoon character and a “strange request” affect a reader?
items.explain:
Step 1. Paragraph 1 describes a cartoon mail carrier and a “strange request.” Paragraph 2 then begins “For most of the nation's history” and goes back in time.

Step 2. A smiling cartoon and an odd new habit make readers curious: why did Americans need this number? The rest of the passage answers that. The correct choice is the one about catching the reader's interest with a memorable moment.

Step 3. The code was not accepted immediately (paragraph 5), the author never says Mr. ZIP was the main reason it succeeded, and the passage never says hand sorting was faster.
options: to catch the reader's interest with a memorable moment, then explain the history behind it
to show that Americans accepted the ZIP Code immediately, on the same day it was introduced
to argue that a cartoon character was the most important reason the ZIP Code succeeded
to prove that sorting by hand was faster than sorting by number when clerks were skilled
why: This contradicts the text. Paragraph 1 calls the code “a strange request” in 1963, and paragraph 5 says many people ignored it at first.
The author never ranks the reasons the code succeeded. Paragraph 5 credits the 1967 requirement and businesses adopting the codes, not Mr. ZIP.
The passage never claims hand sorting was faster. Paragraph 3 says hand sorting “could no longer keep up.”

items.prompt:
Read the draft newsletter article. Then choose the word or phrase that best completes each blank in these excerpts.

Paragraph 2, blank (A): {{0}} the shift ends in the middle of the afternoon, day-shift workers usually have their evenings free for family, classes, or a second job.

Paragraph 3, blank (B): {{1}} the day shift, it is quieter, with fewer trucks and more time spent restocking shelves and preparing orders for the morning.

Paragraph 4, blank (C): An employee who is saving for a car might choose nights for the extra pay, while a parent who wants to be home for dinner might choose days. {{2}} the choice comes down to whether extra pay or a daytime schedule matters more to you.
items.hint: For each blank, decide the relationship: a cause, a difference, or a summing up.
items.explain:
Blank (A). Ending in mid-afternoon is the reason day workers have free evenings: cause and effect. “Since” introduces a cause. “Even though” is tempting, but nothing here is surprising.

Blank (B). The writer is setting the night shift beside the day shift and naming a difference (quieter, fewer trucks). “Unlike” signals contrast.

Blank (C). After two examples, the writer sums up the main point. “In short,” signals a summary. “For instance” is tempting, but the examples came in the sentence before.

options: Since
Even though
Unless
Until
why: “Even though” signals a surprise or contrast. A mid-afternoon finish does not work against having free evenings; it is the reason for them.
“Unless” turns the sentence into a condition (“if the shift does not end”), which reverses the meaning.
“Until” sets a time limit (“up to the time the shift ends”), which does not make sense with free evenings.

options: Unlike
Like
Because of
Similar to
why: “Like” says the night shift is the same as the day shift, but the sentence describes how it differs: quieter, fewer trucks.
“Because of” says the day shift causes the night shift to be quiet. The sentence compares the two shifts; it does not give a cause.
“Similar to” signals a likeness, but the day shift is busy and fast-paced while the night shift is quieter. That is a difference.

options: In short,
For instance,
Meanwhile,
Otherwise,
why: “For instance” introduces an example, but the examples (the car saver and the parent) come in the sentence before. This sentence sums them up.
“Meanwhile” signals two things happening at the same time. The sentence draws a conclusion; it does not move through time.
“Otherwise” means “if not,” a condition the paragraph never sets up.

items.prompt: How does the writer organize paragraphs 2 and 3 of the draft article?
items.hint: Paragraph 1 says the two shifts “differ.” What does each of the next two paragraphs describe?
items.explain:
Step 1. Label each paragraph. Paragraph 2: the day shift (hours, pace, free evenings, seniority). Paragraph 3: the night shift (hours, pace, extra pay, effect on sleep).

Step 2. Paragraph 1 says the shifts “differ,” and paragraph 3 compares directly with the day shift. One subject per paragraph is a block comparison.

Step 3. No step-by-step tasks, no shortage, and sleep is only one detail.
options: by describing one shift in each paragraph so that readers can compare the two
by listing, in time order, everything a worker does from the start of a shift to its end
by describing a shortage of night workers in paragraph 2 and a way to fix it in paragraph 3
by explaining the causes of trouble sleeping in paragraph 2 and its effects on workers in paragraph 3
why: The paragraphs give start and end times, but they never walk through a worker's tasks in order. Each describes a whole shift.
You looked for a problem and a fix, but no shortage is mentioned. The extra $2.00 is a feature of the night shift, not a solution.
You built on one detail: sleep is mentioned once, in paragraph 3, as a drawback of nights. It is not the organizing idea of both paragraphs.

items.prompt: Paragraph 5 first describes how people resisted the new codes and then turns to what the Post Office did anyway. Type the one word in paragraph 5 that signals this turn.
items.hint: Look for a contrast word that means “in spite of that.”
items.explain: Paragraph 5 opens with the resistance: people ignored the codes, some “complained,” and others saw no reason to change. Then the next sentence begins “Nevertheless, the Post Office kept up its campaign.” Nevertheless means “in spite of that”: it signals a contrast with what came before. “At first” is tempting because it starts the paragraph, but it signals time.

mistakes.why: “At first” tells when people ignored the codes; it is a time signal. The word that turns away from the resistance starts the third sentence.
“Complained” describes what some writers did. It is part of the resistance, not a signal word that turns away from it.
“Simply” describes how others saw no reason to change. Look for the contrast word that introduces what the Post Office did in spite of the resistance.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the point of view from which the story is told?
items.hint: Who says “I” in the story? Does the story ever tell us directly what Andre is thinking?
items.explain:
Step 1. The narrator uses “I” and “my” (“my son Andre,” “I was tired”), so the story is in the first person.

Step 2. Identify the narrator: Andre's father, Ray (Denise calls him “Ray,” and he calls Andre “my son”).

Step 3. Ask what he can know. He shares his own suspicions and plans, but he can only watch Andre and overhear him. The omniscient choice is tempting because several characters appear, but we enter only Ray's mind.
options: It is told in the first person by a father who shares his suspicions but can only guess at his son's plans.
It is told in the third person by a narrator who reveals the thoughts of Ray, Andre, and Denise in turn.
It is told in the first person by Andre, who explains to readers why he kept his evening plans a secret.
It is told in the third person by Denise, who hears all about her brother's worries during their phone calls.
why: The narrator says “I” and “my son,” so the story is in the first person. We never learn what Andre or Denise is thinking.
The “I” calls Andre “my son,” so the narrator is the father. Andre never explains himself; we learn his plans only from the note.
Denise speaks to the narrator, who calls her “my sister.” She is a character, not the storyteller, and the narrator says “I.”

items.prompt:
Complete the statement about the passage.

In paragraph 5, the author {{0}}. Paragraph 6 then {{1}}.
items.hint: Give paragraphs 5 and 6 a short label each. Whose views are in paragraph 5?
items.explain:
Paragraph 5. Label it: “resistance, then acceptance.” People ignored and criticized the codes; “Nevertheless,” the Post Office kept going, required codes on bulk mail in 1967, and letter writers followed. The tempting wrong answer copies the critics' complaint as if it were the author's.

Paragraph 6. Label it: “results: machines, ZIP+4, today.” It shows the long-term results. The last sentence looks back at the problem only to sum up.

options: describes resistance to the new codes and how the Post Office overcame it
argues that the government was wrong to turn its citizens into numbers
compares the ZIP Code with the 1943 city zones to show which worked better
lists the steps that businesses followed to add codes to their mailing lists
why: This is the complaint of “some writers,” which the author reports. The author then turns with “Nevertheless” to show the codes won out.
The comparison of the city zones and the ZIP Code is in paragraph 4, not paragraph 5.
Paragraph 5 says only that companies added the codes; it gives no steps for doing so.

options: shows the long-term results of the ZIP Code system
returns to the strain on hand sorting during the war
gives more of the critics' reasons for ignoring the codes
explains how the first digit of each code was chosen
why: Paragraph 6 mentions “an overwhelming problem” only in its last sentence, to sum up. Its main job is what the code made possible afterward.
The critics do not appear in paragraph 6. It moves forward to machines, ZIP+4 in 1983, and today.
What the digits stand for is explained in paragraph 4. Paragraph 6 is about later results.

items.prompt: For most of the story, Ray believes Andre is hiding something bad. Which two details, given before the ending, turn out to be clues that Andre was studying? Select two answers.
items.hint: Reread the ending first. Then look back: which earlier details fit someone going to class and preparing for a test?
items.explain:
Step 1. Read the ending: Andre was attending the Adult Learning Center and passed four subjects. Now look back for clues that point to studying.

Step 2. A backpack is what a student carries; Ray even wonders why a grown man needs one at a friend's house. Correct.

Step 3. “I don't think I'm ready” makes sense for someone nervous about a test. Correct.

Step 4. Kevin's look is the most tempting wrong answer: it is a real clue, but it shows only that Andre lied about where he went. Denise's advice and eating at the counter do not point to studying.
options: Andre takes his backpack with him on Tuesday and Thursday evenings.
On the phone, Andre says, “I don't think I'm ready.”
Kevin looks puzzled when Ray asks how their Tuesdays are going.
Denise tells Ray to let Andre have his business.
Andre eats standing at the counter when he gets home.
why: Kevin's puzzled look shows that Andre was not at Kevin's house. It proves Andre was hiding where he went, but it gives no hint of what he was doing there.
Denise's advice is about respecting Andre's privacy. It tells us nothing about what Andre was doing.
Eating at the counter shows Andre came home late and hungry. It does not point to studying.

items.skill: Effect of narrator's point of view
items.prompt: How does the first-person point of view affect the reader's experience of the story?
items.hint: What does Ray believe for most of the story? When do readers learn something that changes that belief?
items.explain:
Step 1. In first person, readers see only Ray's thoughts. For most of the story, he believes Andre is lying about something bad and plans to confront him.

Step 2. Andre's thoughts are never shown. Readers learn the truth only when Ray finds the report and the note.

Step 3. The point of view creates a surprise and shows the gap between what Ray believes and what is true. The choice saying readers cannot trust any event is tempting, but misjudging a person does not make every reported event false.
options: Readers know only Ray's thoughts, so they share his fear that Andre is in trouble until the report reveals the truth.
Ray explains Andre's thoughts throughout, so readers know from the start that Andre is preparing for his exams.
Ray is upset, so readers cannot trust any of the events he describes, including the report on the kitchen table.
The story is told by Denise, so readers learn how every member of the family really feels about Andre's choices.
why: A first-person narrator cannot see into another character's mind, and Ray never does. Readers learn Andre's plans only from the note at the end.
This goes too far. Ray misjudges his son, but he reports events like the report and the note plainly, and nothing suggests they are false.
Denise is Ray's sister, a character who speaks to him on the phone. The “I” who tells the story is Ray.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the author's point of view toward the ZIP Code?
items.hint: Reread the last sentence of the passage. How does the author describe the ZIP Code in the author's own voice?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the author's own words. The conclusion calls the ZIP Code “a simple answer to what had become an overwhelming problem.” These word choices show approval.

Step 2. Look at how the critics are treated. Paragraph 5 reports that “some writers complained,” then turns with “Nevertheless.” The author reports the objection but does not adopt it.

Step 3. The critics choice confuses their view with the author's. The 1943 zones were only a partial fix, and the claim that the code was unnecessary ignores paragraph 3.
options: The author sees the ZIP Code as a practical fix for a real problem and reports its critics without agreeing.
The author agrees with the critics that the ZIP Code turned American citizens into nothing more than numbers.
The author believes the 1943 city zones worked better than the ZIP Code and should have been kept instead.
The author thinks the ZIP Code was unnecessary because skilled clerks could already sort the mail by memory.
why: You took the critics' words as the author's. The author reports the complaint and then turns with “Nevertheless” to show the codes succeeded.
This contradicts paragraph 4: the zones “did nothing to speed mail moving between cities and towns,” which is why a nationwide plan was needed.
This distorts paragraph 2. Hand sorting worked only while mail stayed manageable and clerks stayed; paragraph 3 says it “could no longer keep up.”

items.skill: Purpose of a part; narrator's point of view
items.prompt:
Complete the statements about the story.

The author ends the story with the note Andre left in order to {{0}}. Because the story is told in the first person, readers learn what Andre was really doing only when {{1}}.
items.hint: What does the note tell Ray that he did not know? In a first-person story, when can readers learn something?
items.explain:
Blank 1. The note answers the story's question (where Andre goes) and adds something new: “Your turn, Pop.” Andre, who left school in the eleventh grade, has finished what he started, and now he is inviting his father to take the same step. The note reveals the truth and shows Andre's hope for his father. Saying Ray was right all along is tempting, but it ignores that the secret was good news.

Blank 2. The narrator is Ray, so readers know only what he learns. The truth comes out only when Ray finds the report and the note.

options: reveal the truth about Andre's evenings and show what he hopes for his father
show that Andre plans to move out of his father's house in January
prove that Ray had been right all along to be suspicious of his son
introduce a new conflict between Andre and his aunt Denise
why: This goes beyond the text. “A spot for you in January” is a place in a class for Ray; nothing says Andre is moving out.
This distorts the ending. Ray was right that Andre had a secret, but wrong that it was something bad. The note shows the secret was good news.
Denise does not appear at the end, and the note is addressed to Ray. The story closes here; no new conflict begins.

options: Ray finds the report and the note
Andre explains his thoughts to readers
Denise tells Ray the truth on the phone
Kevin describes their Tuesday evenings
why: Andre never narrates and never explains himself. In a first-person story, readers stay inside Ray's mind.
Denise only tells Ray to let Andre have his business. She never reveals anything about Andre's evenings.
Kevin never describes anything. His puzzled look shows only that Andre was not at his house.

stimuli.title: Keep the Library Rolling
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] Every Saturday morning in the parking lot of the Linden Street laundromat, a converted delivery truck opens its side door and unfolds a small set of steps. Within minutes, a line forms: children holding last week's picture books, a retired bus driver looking for mysteries, a young mother who needs a computer to apply for jobs. The truck is the Carver County Mobile Library, and for many of these families, it is the only library they can reach.

[2] The county's one library building sits downtown, almost nine miles from the farthest neighborhoods. No bus line runs there on weekends. For families without a car, or with parents who work long weekday shifts, a library card is close to useless.

[3] The mobile library was the county's answer. Since it began in 2022, it has made eleven regular stops a week, carrying about 2,000 books, six laptops, and a wireless hotspot. Last year, it checked out more than 30,000 items, and nearly half of its users said they had never had a library card before.

[4] Some county commissioners now want to cut the program to save its yearly cost of $140,000. They point out, correctly, that a building lasts for decades while a truck wears out. But that argument counts only what the program costs, not what it delivers. Divided among the 30,000 items it lent last year, the truck costs less than five dollars per item, a bargain for families who would otherwise go without.

[5] The commissioners should keep the mobile library running and, if anything, add stops. A library that people cannot reach is only a building. A library that comes to them is a lifeline.

stimuli.title: The Red Ribbon
stimuli.source: Original fiction written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] Mrs. Petrakis watches everything. When I get home from school, her curtain moves. When I take out the trash, her porch light snaps on, even in daylight. Last week I let my friend Jaylen in at four, and by five my mother had called me from work to ask, in her careful voice, who was over.

[2] I know who told her.

[3] So on Friday, when my key snapped off in the lock and I was stuck on the porch in the rain, I would have waited until midnight before knocking on her door. I did not have to. Her door opened before I reached the steps. She was holding a towel, a plate of something warm, and a brass key on a red ribbon.

[4] “Your mother gave me this in September,” she said. “She said, ‘Just in case. You'll know when.’”

[5] I took the key. Behind her, on the windowsill, a small notebook lay open. On the page, in blue ink: 3:42, home. 3:50, light on. OK.

stimuli.title: The Bus with No Wheels
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] At 7:45 on a typical school morning two years ago, the street in front of Hillview Elementary turned into a parking lot. Cars idled two lanes deep, horns sounded, and a lone crossing guard waved children between bumpers. Most of those cars carried one child each, and many of those children lived less than a mile from the school.

[2] It was not always this way. In 1969, nearly half of American children ages 5 to 14 walked or biked to school. By 2009, only about 13 percent did. Parents who drive often say the walk is too dangerous because of traffic, yet every parent who drives adds one more car to the crowd at the curb, making the walk more dangerous for everyone else.

[3] That fall, Hillview parents tried a simple answer: the walking school bus. Like a bus, it follows a set route and picks up children at marked “stops” along the way, but it travels on foot, with one adult volunteer in the lead and another at the rear. Hillview now runs three routes, and about 70 children walk each morning. The school counts about 50 fewer cars in the drop-off line each day.

[4] Skeptics warn that programs like this depend on volunteers, and volunteers are hard to find. That concern is fair; a route with no adults cannot run. Yet Hillview's routes have not missed a single morning, because the school asks each family to lead just one walk a month. When the job is small, people say yes.

[5] Every school with a clogged curb should give the walking school bus a try. It costs almost nothing, it gets children moving before the first bell, and it turns a daily traffic jam back into what a trip to school should be: a walk with friends.

stimuli.title: Monday at Seven
stimuli.source: Original fiction written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] Tasha had rehearsed her answers on the bus, twice, under her breath, until the man across the aisle moved to another seat. Now, across the desk from the hiring manager, she could not remember a single one.

[2] Mr. Albright read her application without looking up. He frowned at the first page. He frowned harder at the second. When she explained the two-year gap in her work history, the months she had spent caring for her grandmother, he set down his pen and stared out the window, and Tasha felt the job slip away like a bus pulling from the curb.

[3] She was reaching for her bag when he finally spoke.

[4] “My father had a stroke a few years back,” he said. “I was the one who learned to give him his medicine, too.” He slid a paper across the desk. “We start new hires on Mondays. Can you be here at seven?”

items.prompt: Which statement best describes how the passage as a whole is organized?
items.explain: Label the paragraphs: [1] hook (the Saturday line); [2] the problem (the only library is nine miles away, no weekend bus); [3] the solution and its results (eleven stops, 30,000 items); [4] the commissioners' objection and the author's answer; [5] a call to action. The structure is problem and solution, with an objection answered and a call to act. The compare choice is tempting because two libraries are mentioned, but the downtown building appears only to show the problem.
options: It describes a problem with library access, explains a solution, answers an objection, and urges action.
It tells the history of the county library in time order, from the day it opened to the present year.
It compares the downtown library and the mobile library point by point to show which one costs the county less.
It explains the causes of falling reading rates and the effects they have on families in the county.
why: The passage gives one date (2022), but it never traces the library's history. Its paragraphs do the jobs of problem, solution, objection, and call to action.
The downtown building is mentioned only to show the problem (it is too far away). The author never compares the two libraries' costs.
Reading rates are never mentioned. The problem in paragraph 2 is distance and transportation, not falling reading rates.

items.skill: Author's point of view: the turn
items.prompt: Click the sentence in paragraph 4 where the author begins to answer the commissioners' argument.
items.explain: Sentences 1 and 2 give the commissioners' view; the word “correctly” shows the author admitting part of it is true. Sentence 3 turns with “But” and begins the author's answer: the commissioners count only cost, not what the program delivers. Sentence 4 supports that answer with numbers ($140,000 ÷ 30,000 is about $4.67 per item).
spans: Some county commissioners now want to cut the program to save its yearly cost of $140,000.
They point out, correctly, that a building lasts for decades while a truck wears out.
But that argument counts only what the program costs, not what it delivers.
Divided among the 30,000 items it lent last year, the truck costs less than five dollars per item, a bargain for families who would otherwise go without.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence with “correctly.” There the author admits the commissioners have a point (a concession); the answer begins with “But.”

items.prompt: Why does the author begin the passage with the scene in the laundromat parking lot?
items.explain: The opening shows a line forming within minutes: children, a retired bus driver, a young mother who needs a computer. The last sentence says the truck is “the only library they can reach.” Opening with real people hooks the reader and makes the stakes concrete before the author explains the problem and the cost debate. The step-by-step choice is tempting because the truck “unfolds a small set of steps,” but the paragraph is a scene, not a set of instructions.
options: to catch the reader's interest by showing real people who depend on the mobile library
to explain step by step how the library staff sets up the truck at each of its stops
to argue that the county should build a new library beside the Linden Street laundromat
to compare the people who use the mobile library with those who visit the main building
why: You focused on the truck's door and steps, but they are part of a scene, not instructions. The paragraph's real focus is the line of people.
This is not stated. The author asks the county to keep the truck and add stops, never to build a library at the laundromat.
The paragraph describes only the people in line at the truck; no visitors to the downtown building are described.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement about the passage.

Paragraph 2 {{0}}, and paragraph 3 {{1}}.
items.explain: Paragraph 2: the library is nine miles away, no weekend bus, a card is “close to useless.” Label: the problem. Paragraph 3 opens “The mobile library was the county's answer” and gives results (11 stops, 30,000 items, half had never had a card). Label: the solution and evidence. The objection is in paragraph 4 and the call to action in paragraph 5.

options: describes the problem that the mobile library was created to solve
presents the commissioners' reasons for cutting the program
explains how the mobile library chooses its eleven stops
compares the cost of a library building with the cost of a truck
why: The commissioners appear in paragraph 4. Paragraph 2 explains why many families could not reach a library.
Paragraph 2 never mentions stops; it is about the distance to the one library building and the lack of weekend buses.
Costs come up in paragraph 4. Paragraph 2 is about distance and transportation.

options: explains the solution and gives evidence that it works
answers an objection raised by people who disagree
urges readers to contact their county commissioners
returns to the scene in the laundromat parking lot
why: The objection and the author's answer come in paragraph 4. Paragraph 3 describes the program and its results.
The call to action is in paragraph 5, and it is aimed at the commissioners, not at readers contacting them.
Paragraph 3 never mentions the laundromat. It gives numbers about the whole program.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the author's point of view toward cutting the mobile library?
items.explain: The author's own words show the position: the program is “a bargain,” the commissioners “should keep the mobile library running and, if anything, add stops,” and the truck is “a lifeline.” The author also admits the commissioners point out “correctly” that a building outlasts a truck, but answers that they count only cost. So the author opposes the cut while conceding one point. The second-building choice is tempting because buildings are mentioned, but that was the commissioners' comparison, not the author's proposal.
options: The author opposes the cut, admitting one point the commissioners make but arguing the benefits are worth the cost.
The author agrees with the commissioners that the mobile library has simply become too expensive to keep running.
The author thinks the county should replace the truck with a second library building that would last for decades.
The author takes no side and simply reports what the commissioners and the families each say about the program.
why: You took the commissioners' view as the author's. The author answers it with “But” and ends by saying the program should be kept.
This is not stated. The point about buildings lasting longer is the commissioners'; the author never proposes a second building.
“A bargain,” “a lifeline,” and “should keep the mobile library running” are clear judgments. The author takes a side.

items.skill: Author's point of view: word choice
items.prompt: Which two phrases most clearly reveal the author's attitude toward the mobile library? Select two answers.
items.explain: “A bargain” judges the cost as well worth paying, and “a lifeline” presents the library as something families depend on to survive. Swap them for neutral words (“costs about $4.67 per item,” “is a service”) and the approval disappears. The other phrases are facts any writer could use; the $140,000 figure is the commissioners' concern, not the author's attitude.
options: “a bargain for families who would otherwise go without”
“A library that comes to them is a lifeline.”
“a converted delivery truck opens its side door”
“carrying about 2,000 books, six laptops, and a wireless hotspot”
“to save its yearly cost of $140,000”
why: This is a neutral description of the truck. Any writer, for or against the program, could describe it this way.
These are neutral facts about what the truck carries. They inform without judging.
This states the commissioners' goal and the program's cost. It is a fact, not the author's attitude.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the point of view from which the story is told?
items.explain: The narrator uses “I” and “my mother” and describes getting home from school, so the story is in the first person, told by a young person. Mrs. Petrakis is seen only from outside: her curtain moves, her porch light snaps on, she opens the door. The narrator reports her actions and words but cannot see her reasons. The omniscient choice is tempting because the ending explains her behavior, but that explanation comes from what she says and the notebook, not from her thoughts.
options: It is told in the first person by a young person who sees what Mrs. Petrakis does but cannot know why.
It is told in the third person by a narrator who reveals what both Mrs. Petrakis and the young person think.
It is told in the first person by Mrs. Petrakis, who explains why she keeps a notebook about the house next door.
It is told in the third person by the young person's mother, who hears about her child's day from a neighbor.
why: The narrator says “I” and “my mother,” so the story is in the first person. We never read Mrs. Petrakis's thoughts, only what she does and says.
The “I” describes Mrs. Petrakis from outside (“her curtain moves”), so the narrator cannot be her. She never explains the notebook.
The mother appears only in a phone call and in what Mrs. Petrakis reports. The storyteller is the “I” who gets home from school.

items.skill: Effect of narrator's point of view
items.prompt: How does the first-person point of view affect the reader's understanding of Mrs. Petrakis?
items.explain: For most of the story the narrator believes Mrs. Petrakis is spying (“I know who told her”). Because we see only the narrator's thoughts, we share that belief. The ending changes it: the mother gave her a key “just in case,” and the notebook (“home… light on. OK.”) shows she was checking that the narrator was safe. The point of view creates the surprise. The choice saying readers cannot trust any event is tempting, but misjudging a person does not make every event false.
options: Readers share the narrator's view of her as a spy until the key and notebook show she was watching over the narrator.
Readers know from the start that the mother asked her to keep watch, because the narrator explains her thoughts.
Readers cannot trust any event the narrator reports, including the broken key, because the narrator is so annoyed.
Readers learn what every neighbor on the street thinks of her, because the narrator describes all of their opinions.
why: A first-person narrator cannot read her mind, and the mother's request is revealed only at the end, when Mrs. Petrakis explains the key.
This goes too far. The narrator misjudges Mrs. Petrakis's reasons, but events like the broken key and the open door are reported plainly.
No other neighbors appear in the story. The narrator shares only one view, the narrator's own.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes how the passage as a whole is organized?
items.explain: Label the paragraphs: [1] hook and problem (the traffic jam); [2] background (fewer children walk; driving makes walking more dangerous); [3] the solution and results (three routes, 50 fewer cars); [4] the skeptics' objection and the author's answer; [5] a call to action. The structure is problem and solution, with an objection answered. The history choice is tempting because of the dates in paragraph 2, but they are only background.
options: It describes a traffic problem, explains a solution, answers an objection, and urges other schools to act.
It tells the history of school transportation in time order, from the year 1969 up to the present day.
It compares walking and biking to school point by point to show which is safer for young children.
It explains the causes of childhood health problems and the effects they have on students' learning.
why: The passage gives two dates in paragraph 2 as background, but it does not trace a history. Its paragraphs do the jobs of problem, solution, objection, and call to action.
Walking and biking are mentioned together once, in a statistic. The passage never weighs one against the other.
Health is touched on only in “gets children moving.” The problem the passage describes is traffic at the curb.

items.skill: Author's point of view: the turn
items.prompt: Click the sentence in paragraph 4 where the author begins to answer the skeptics.
items.explain: Sentence 1 gives the skeptics' view. Sentence 2 is a concession: the author agrees the concern is fair. Sentence 3 turns with “Yet” and gives the author's answer: Hillview has never missed a morning because each family leads only one walk a month. Sentence 4 states the lesson of that answer.
spans: Skeptics warn that programs like this depend on volunteers, and volunteers are hard to find.
That concern is fair; a route with no adults cannot run.
Yet Hillview's routes have not missed a single morning, because the school asks each family to lead just one walk a month.
When the job is small, people say yes.
items.why: The most common wrong click is “That concern is fair.” There the author admits the skeptics have a point (a concession); the answer begins with “Yet.”

items.prompt: Why does the author begin the passage with the scene in front of Hillview Elementary?
items.explain: The opening paints the problem vividly: cars two lanes deep, horns, a lone crossing guard, and many children living less than a mile away. That scene hooks the reader and sets up the problem the walking school bus answers in paragraph 3. Paragraph 2 then steps back to explain how things got this way. The crossing-guard choice is tempting because the guard is in the scene, but the author never proposes more guards.
options: to catch the reader's interest by showing the problem the rest of the passage tries to solve
to explain step by step how a crossing guard should guide children safely between cars
to argue that the school should hire more crossing guards to handle the morning traffic
to compare the children who walk to Hillview with the children who ride the school bus
why: The crossing guard is one detail in the scene. The paragraph gives no instructions; it shows how bad the traffic was.
This is not stated. The author's answer to the traffic is the walking school bus, not more crossing guards.
No real school bus or walking children appear in the opening; it shows cars carrying one child each.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement about the passage.

Paragraph 2 {{0}}, and paragraph 3 {{1}}.
items.explain: Paragraph 2: walking fell from nearly half of children in 1969 to about 13 percent in 2009, and each parent who drives makes walking more dangerous. Label: background, how the problem grew. Paragraph 3 introduces “a simple answer: the walking school bus” and reports results (70 children, 50 fewer cars). Label: the solution and evidence. The skeptics come in paragraph 4 and the call to action in paragraph 5.

options: gives background on how the problem grew and why it keeps getting worse
presents the skeptics' reasons for doubting the walking school bus
explains how Hillview chose the stops for its three walking routes
compares the cost of driving with the cost of walking to school
why: The skeptics appear in paragraph 4. Paragraph 2 explains the decline in walking and the cycle of driving.
Paragraph 2 never mentions Hillview's routes; it gives national numbers and explains a cycle.
Cost is never compared in paragraph 2. It is about how many children walk and why.

options: describes a solution and gives evidence that it works
answers a concern raised by people who disagree
urges readers to start programs at their own schools
returns to the history of walking to school since 1969
why: The concern and the author's answer come in paragraph 4. Paragraph 3 describes the program and its results.
The call to action is in paragraph 5. Paragraph 3 reports what Hillview did and what happened.
The 1969 figures are in paragraph 2. Paragraph 3 is about Hillview's walking school bus.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the author's point of view toward the walking school bus?
items.explain: The author calls the program “a simple answer,” says it “costs almost nothing,” and urges every school with a clogged curb to try it. In paragraph 4 the author admits the volunteer concern “is fair,” then answers it: one walk a month per family has kept every route running. So the author supports the program while conceding one point. The replace-every-bus choice is tempting because of the title and the bus comparison, but the author never suggests replacing real buses.
options: The author supports it, admitting the volunteer concern is fair but arguing that it can be solved.
The author agrees with the skeptics that the program asks far too much of busy parent volunteers.
The author thinks the program should replace every school bus route in the district within a year.
The author takes no side and simply reports what the parents and the skeptics each say about it.
why: You took the skeptics' view as the author's. The author calls the concern fair, then answers it with “Yet” and the one-walk-a-month plan.
This is not stated. The author never mentions replacing school bus routes; the program is compared with a bus only to explain how it works.
“A simple answer,” “costs almost nothing,” and “should give the walking school bus a try” show a clear side.

items.skill: Author's point of view: word choice
items.prompt: Which two phrases most clearly reveal the author's attitude toward the walking school bus? Select two answers.
items.explain: “A simple answer” presents the program as an easy, sensible fix, and “what a trip to school should be: a walk with friends” shows the author's warm view of the goal. Both are judgments. The number of routes, the volunteers' positions, and the 1969 statistic are facts any writer could use, whatever the writer's opinion.
options: “tried a simple answer”
“what a trip to school should be: a walk with friends”
“Hillview now runs three routes”
“one adult volunteer in the lead and another at the rear”
“In 1969, nearly half of American children”
why: This is a neutral fact about the program's size. It informs without judging.
This neutrally describes how the walk is organized. Any writer could include it.
This is a statistic that gives background. It does not show how the author feels about the program.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the point of view from which the story is told?
items.explain: The narrator uses “she” and “he,” so the story is in the third person. Then count the minds: we learn that Tasha “could not remember a single one” of her answers and “felt the job slip away,” but Mr. Albright is shown only through actions (reading, frowning, staring) and his final words. One mind means third person limited. The first-person choice is tempting because we feel close to Tasha, but the narrator never says “I.”
options: It is told in the third person, and the narrator shares Tasha's thoughts while showing Mr. Albright only from outside.
It is told in the first person by Tasha, who describes her own interview and how she felt as it went along.
It is told in the third person, and the narrator moves back and forth between Tasha's thoughts and Mr. Albright's thoughts.
It is told in the first person by Mr. Albright, who explains to readers why he decided to hire Tasha after all.
why: The narrator calls her “Tasha” and “she,” never “I.” We are close to her thoughts, but the telling is in the third person.
We see Mr. Albright frown and stare out the window, but we never learn what he is thinking until he speaks. Only Tasha's mind is shown.
Mr. Albright is “he” and is seen from outside. He speaks only at the end, inside quotation marks.

items.skill: Effect of narrator's point of view
items.prompt: How does the point of view affect the reader's understanding of the interview?
items.explain: Because the narrator shows only Tasha's thoughts, readers read Mr. Albright's frowns and silence the way she does: as signs she is failing. His thoughts stay hidden until he speaks about caring for his own father, which shows that her caregiving gap made him sympathetic, not doubtful. The limited point of view builds the tension and the surprise. The choice saying readers cannot trust any event is tempting, but misreading someone's frown does not make the job offer false.
options: Readers share Tasha's belief that the interview is going badly until Mr. Albright's words reveal what he was thinking.
Readers know from the start that Mr. Albright plans to hire Tasha, because the narrator reveals his private thoughts.
Readers cannot trust any event in the story, including the job offer, because Tasha is far too nervous to see clearly.
Readers see the interview from an outsider's view, because the story is told by the man who sat across the aisle.
why: The narrator never enters Mr. Albright's mind. His frowns seem bad until he explains his own experience at the end.
This goes too far. Tasha misreads Mr. Albright's frowns, but the events, including the offer, are reported plainly.
The man on the bus appears only in the first sentence and does not tell the story. The narrator stays close to Tasha.

vocab.def: The pattern an author uses to organize ideas in a text.
vocab.example: A history article that tells events in the order they happened uses chronological structure.

vocab.def: Organizing events or steps in the order they happen in time. Also called time order or sequence.
vocab.example: First the dough rises; then it is shaped; finally it is baked.

vocab.def: A structure that explains why something happened (the cause) and what happened as a result (the effect).
vocab.example: Because the road flooded, the school canceled classes.

vocab.def: A structure that shows how two or more things are alike (compare) and different (contrast).
vocab.example: Both jobs pay weekly; however, only one offers health insurance.

vocab.def: A structure that describes a problem and one or more ways it was or could be solved.
vocab.example: Long lines at the clinic were cut in half when it began taking appointments online.

vocab.def: Words or phrases that show how ideas are connected. Also called transitions.
vocab.example: As a result signals an effect; in contrast signals a difference.

vocab.def: The reason an author writes a text or includes a part of it: to inform or explain, to persuade, or to entertain.
vocab.example: A safety guide is written to explain how to use a ladder correctly.

vocab.def: A short story about a real event, often used to open a text and catch the reader's interest.
vocab.example: An article on job training begins with one worker's first day in a new career.

vocab.def: The author's position or attitude toward a subject, shown through word choice, what is included, and the conclusion.
vocab.example: Calling a plan “wasteful” shows the author opposes it.

vocab.def: A position that disagrees with the author's. Authors often present it and then answer it.
vocab.example: “Some say the fee is too high. However, …”

vocab.def: The voice that tells a story. The narrator may or may not be a character in it.
vocab.example: In a story that begins “I never meant to leave home,” the narrator is a character.

vocab.def: A story told by a narrator who is a character and uses “I” or “we.” Readers know only what that narrator knows.
vocab.example: “I thought the call was bad news, so I let it ring.”

vocab.def: A story told with “he,” “she,” or “they” that shares the thoughts of only one character.
vocab.example: “Marcus wondered whether his sister was still angry.”

vocab.def: A story told by an all-knowing narrator who shares the thoughts of many characters.
vocab.example: “Marcus wondered whether his sister was still angry. She had already forgotten the argument.”

vocab.def: A point where an author admits that part of an opposing view is true, usually before answering it. Admitting a point is not the same as agreeing overall.
vocab.example: “It is true that pools are expensive to run. But…”

notes:
Week 3 RLA Study Sheet: Text Structure, Author's Purpose, Point of View

Text structures

StructureJobSignal words
ChronologicalEvents or steps in orderfirst, next, then, later, finally, before, after, dates
Cause and effectWhy it happened; what it led tobecause, since, so, as a result, therefore, led to, due to
Compare and contrastAlike and differentboth, similarly, however, unlike, in contrast, while, on the other hand
Problem and solutionWhat went wrong; how to fix itproblem, challenge, solution, answer, proposed, solved

Finding the structure

  1. Note the scope: sentence, paragraph, or passage.
  2. Circle signal words.
  3. Label each paragraph's job.
  4. Pick the structure that fits all of them.

Opens out of order? A dramatic first scene is a hook. Use dates, not paragraph order.

Compare and contrast: block (one subject per paragraph) or point by point (one feature at a time).

Author's purpose

  • Inform/explain, persuade, entertain
  • Frame: “to ___ readers about ___”
  • Purpose of a part: hook, example/evidence, contrast, opposing view, result

Author's point of view clues

  • Word choice (reckless vs. bold)
  • What is included or left out
  • How opponents are treated (find the turn: but, however, yet; a concession is not agreement)
  • The conclusion

Narrator's point of view

  • First person: “I”; only the narrator's mind; may be mistaken
  • Third limited: “he/she”; one character's thoughts
  • Third omniscient: many characters' thoughts

Count the minds. Effect = what the narrator believes vs. what the details show.

Key idea: Signal words are clues, not proof. Ask what job each paragraph is doing.

Strategy: Label each paragraph in two to four words before answering. Look before and after a part to find its purpose.

Common mistakes: choosing a structure from one signal word; answering about the whole passage when asked about one part; picking a vague purpose; assuming the author agrees with everyone quoted; trusting a first-person narrator completely.
